Off-road drivers heading beyond the bitumen should add a topographic navigation app such as ExplorOz Traveller to whichever camping app they choose.

sections.heading: 1. AussieCamps: best for official data and trip planning on iPhone
body: AussieCamps is our own app, built for travellers who want to choose tonight's stop and plan the rest of the trip in one place. Its campground, rest area and facility records come from state park agencies, road authorities and public facility datasets such as NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, Parks Victoria, Main Roads WA and the National Public Toilet Map. The current release carries 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas, 1,393 dump points, 3,004 drinking water points and 1,186 public toilets.

The place directory is stored on the phone, so facilities, fees, rules and access notes stay readable after the last bar of signal. Map tiles, directions, weather and photos still need a connection, and there is no offline map. The trip planner orders stops, shows the driving distance and time for each leg, adds arrival dates with a forecast for each stop, and can sync the trip to your calendar.

The download is free and so are the bookable hotels, motels, B&Bs, holiday parks and tours from the booking partner, BookEasy. Campgrounds, rest areas, dump points, water, parks, guides, collections and trips need the AussieCamps Pass, a weekly subscription or a one-off lifetime purchase; the Australian App Store lists its in-app purchases from A$2.99 to A$9.99.

What we like: data with a named official source, details that work with no signal without downloading regions first, and filters for water, toilets, showers, power, dogs and vehicle access. What to weigh: it is iPhone only, it lists fewer places than WikiCamps, and there are no traveller reviews, so you will not see a comment from last week about a muddy access road.
tips: Best for: iPhone users who plan ahead
Weak spot: no Android version, no user reviews
Price: free download, Pass for camping data

sections.heading: 2. WikiCamps Australia: best for the biggest community database
body: WikiCamps has been part of Australian road trips for more than a decade, and its strength is its community. Every listing, photo and review comes from users, and the developer reports more than 65,000 sites, 1.3 million reviews and 900,000 photos. That volume means recent comments on road conditions, mozzies or a broken tap at a free camp, which no official dataset carries.

It costs A$9.99 once, with no subscription, but you pay separately on iPhone and Android. The trip planner estimates fuel cost along a route, and you can book some sites in the app. Offline, it keeps the maps and up to three planned trips available without signal.
What we like: the sheer coverage, honest recent reviews and a single fair price. What to weigh: accuracy depends on users keeping listings current, and the offline limit of three planned trips.
tips: Best for: the widest coverage and recent reviews

sections.heading: 3. CAMPS Australia Wide: best for sites checked in person
body: CAMPS comes from Camps Australia Wide, whose team has been checking sites since 1992. It lists more than 16,000 campsites that the company says are personally checked, with no paid listings. Community reviews sit alongside the editorial data, and the app adds live fuel prices, a trip planner and in-app booking.
Access starts with a 7-day free trial and then costs A$14.99 a year. The paid plan lets you download offline maps with site information, so details stay available without signal once downloaded.

What we like: a curated list from people who visit sites, a long record and a low annual price. What to weigh: the whole app needs a subscription after the trial, a smaller list than WikiCamps, and no computer version for planning on a laptop.
tips: Best for: travellers who trust curated data
Weak spot: annual subscription after a 7-day trial
Price: A$14.99 a year after a trial

sections.heading: 4. CamperMate: best free app for Australia and New Zealand
body: CamperMate covers both sides of the Tasman in one free app, which suits travellers doing Australia and New Zealand on the same trip. It lists more than 70,000 points of interest, including free and paid campsites, holiday parks, dump stations, toilets and wifi, with traveller reviews and photos.
Maps and key information can be downloaded for use without signal. It is available in 27 languages, a real help for visitors whose first language is not English.

What we like: free to use, two countries in one app and wide language support. What to weigh: it mixes camping with general points of interest, its listings are community-contributed with no named official sources, and booking and deal listings sit alongside free options.
tips: Best for: free use across two countries
Weak spot: no named official sources

sections.heading: 5. Hipcamp: best for booking stays on private land
body: Hipcamp is a booking platform rather than a camp finder. Farmers, station owners, vineyards and other landholders list their own campsites, glamping tents and caravan spots, and you book and pay through the app. It is the most highly rated app on this list, with 4.8 stars from more than 22,000 Australian ratings.
The app is free to download and every stay is priced by its host. The app keeps your booked trips and host messages cached for offline access, but you cannot search for new stays without signal.

What we like: unique sites you will not find in public directories, clear photos and reviews, and booking in one place. What to weigh: it is not built for free camps, rest areas or dump points, and most stays need to be booked ahead.
tips: Best for: a planned weekend somewhere unusual
Weak spot: no free camps or road stops
Price: free app, you pay each host

sections.heading: 6. Full Range Camping: best for member discounts
body: Full Range Camping is the current name of FreeRange Camping, a directory of more than 11,000 camping spots and businesses with a large membership. The app is free, and Premium membership is listed at A$49.99 a year or A$99.99 for life. On 20 October 2026 its website said Premium memberships were currently unavailable while the app's mapping software is updated, so check before you plan around it.

Premium adds offline access to the listings, member discounts the company puts at up to 30 per cent at some campgrounds, and weather radar. The same membership opens house sitting and work exchange listings, which long-term travellers use to cut accommodation costs.

What we like: a membership that can pay for itself if you use the discounts, and extras for long trips. What to weigh: offline access needs Premium, and the app has far fewer App Store ratings than the leaders, 262 at the time of checking.
tips: Best for: long trips that use discounts
Weak spot: offline is a paid feature
Price: free, Premium A$49.99 a year

sections.heading: 7. ExplorOz Traveller: best for outback tracks and 4WD touring
body: ExplorOz Traveller is a navigation and touring app first, built around EOTopo, an Australia-wide topographic map with named roads, 4WD tracks and walking and mountain bike trails. The developer lists more than 100,000 places, including camps, fuel and water, so it doubles as a camp finder once you are on a remote track.

The app costs A$59.99, and offline use needs one in-app option: EOTopo Annual Access at A$59.99 a year, EOTopo 2026 4-Year Access at A$79.99, or Pro Access at A$99.99 a year, which also adds live tracking, sharing and GPX export. Once downloaded, the whole Australian map works without signal, which is exactly what a desert crossing needs.

What we like: a full topographic map of the country on the phone and serious detail on tracks most apps do not draw. What to weigh: it has the highest up-front and first-year cost of the apps here, and it is more than most travellers on sealed roads need.
tips: Best for: remote tracks and desert crossings
Weak spot: highest first-year cost here
Price: A$59.99 plus an offline map

sections.heading: How we chose and compared
body: We started from the best-known Australian camping and outback apps, then kept those that help you choose where to stay or how to get there. Each was checked on 20 October 2026 for its Australian App Store price, in-app purchases, rating, platforms and latest update, and against the developer's own description of its data and offline behaviour.

We compared five things: where the data comes from, what still works with no signal, what it costs over a typical trip, how well it turns saved places into a plan, and who it is really for. Ratings are shown as published; a new app such as ours has too few ratings to display, and that is worth knowing.

AussieCamps is paid for by the Pass; free BookEasy listings help keep the download free. No other app on this list paid to be included or had a say in what we wrote. If a price or feature has changed since we checked, tell us through the support page and we will correct it.
tips: Developer claims are quoted as claims
No app paid to be listed

sections.heading: Which app suits which trip
body: Most travellers end up with two apps: one to find places and one for something it does not do, such as booking a farm stay or navigating a 4WD track. The table matches common trips to a starting choice.

sections.heading: Test any camping app before you rely on it
body: Put the phone in flight mode and open a place you have not looked at before. Whatever appears is what you will have out there. Some apps cache map tiles only, others keep place details, and some keep nothing unless you downloaded a region first.

Every app is a planning aid. Fire bans, closures after rain and ranger directions change faster than any dataset, so read the sign at the entrance and check the land manager before settling in. If the sign and the app disagree, the sign wins.
tips: Test offline in flight mode first

faq: What is the best camping app in Australia?

It depends on your phone and how you travel. On iPhone, AussieCamps pairs official campground, rest area and dump point data that stays readable without signal with a full trip planner. WikiCamps Australia has a community-built database of more than 65,000 sites for a one-off A$9.99, and CAMPS lists sites its own team has checked.
Is WikiCamps free?
No. As of October 2026, WikiCamps Australia costs A$9.99 as a one-off purchase on each platform, with no subscription. CamperMate is a free alternative.
Which camping app works without phone signal?

They keep different things. AussieCamps stores place details on the phone with no download step, while map tiles, directions and weather need signal. WikiCamps keeps maps and up to three planned trips, CAMPS and CamperMate let you download maps and site information, and Full Range Camping keeps listings offline with Premium.
Is there a free camping app for Australia?

CamperMate is free, and Hipcamp is free to download with each stay paid to its host. AussieCamps is a free download with free hotel, motel and holiday park listings, but its campground, rest area and dump point data needs the Pass.

australia-travel-cost-2026.title: How much does it really cost to travel Australia in 2026?
australia-travel-cost-2026.description: A practical daily budget for backpackers, campers, road trippers and travellers who want a little more comfort.
australia-travel-cost-2026.imageAlt: Traveller planning an Australian road trip budget
australia-travel-cost-2026.intro: Australia can be travelled leanly, comfortably or extravagantly, but the honest total depends on how often you move. These dated benchmarks combine food, accommodation, local transport and a modest activity allowance before long-distance travel.

sections.heading: Build the daily number from real components
body: Start with the bed or campsite, then add groceries, eating out, local transport and the average cost of paid experiences. Keeping these lines separate makes the estimate easier to update when one part changes.

Vehicle travellers should calculate fuel from kilometres and consumption instead of hiding it inside a daily allowance. A fast lap costs more than a slower trip even when the nightly rate is identical.

sections.heading: Why one Australian average misleads
body: Sydney, remote roadhouses, tropical dry-season towns and school-holiday beaches can all sit above an ordinary regional benchmark. Promotions and longer stays can move the opposite way.
Use the table as a scenario tool, then replace each line with quotes for the dates and route you actually want.

sections.heading: A budget that survives a changed plan
body: Hold at least one legal paid-night option and enough money for an extra tank of fuel. Free camping does not remove the need for showers, laundry, water, repairs or the occasional full-service reset.
Review actual spending every few days. Correcting a small drift in week one is easier than cancelling the best part of the trip in week four.

sections.heading: Where the money actually goes
body: For most road trips the order is vehicle, fuel, food, campsites, activities. Campsites are usually a smaller line than people expect and fuel a much larger one, which is why choosing a slower route saves more than choosing cheaper sites.
That ordering tells you where to look when a budget drifts. Cutting a forty dollar campsite to nothing saves less than removing one five hundred kilometre detour, and it costs you a shower.

Activities are the other quiet line. A reef trip, a scenic flight over Uluru or a Kimberley cruise can each equal several days of ordinary travel, so decide in advance which two or three are worth it.
tips: One detour costs more than many campsites

sections.heading: Costs that only appear once you arrive
body: Vehicle excess reduction, one-way relocation fees, a local SIM, national park passes in several states and the bond held on your card are all real amounts rarely included in a daily budget. Together they add several hundred dollars to a fortnight.

Park passes in particular catch people out. Several states charge vehicle entry separately from camping, and a multi-park pass is usually far better value than daily entries once you visit more than two.
Interstate quarantine also has a small cost: produce disposed of at borders is money spent twice if you shop before crossing rather than after.
tips: Excess reduction is a real cost

sections.heading: Three honest daily budgets
body: A frugal traveller cooking almost everything, mixing free camps and cheap national park sites and driving moderate distances can plan around eighty to a hundred and thirty dollars per person per day before long-distance transport.

A mixed approach with caravan parks every third night, some meals out and a few paid activities lands roughly between a hundred and sixty and two hundred and sixty. A comfort-oriented trip with cabins and regular restaurants moves well beyond that.
None of these include the vehicle itself, flights or a Tasmania crossing. Price those separately, because they are large fixed amounts that distort a daily average.

sections.heading: Making the money work while you are here
body: Contactless card payment is accepted almost everywhere including small regional cafes, and since 1 October 2026 businesses can no longer add a surcharge to eftpos, Mastercard or Visa payments. Cash is still needed for honesty boxes, roadside stalls and some remote roadhouses.

Foreign transaction fees are the quiet drain. A travel card or a bank that does not charge them saves a meaningful amount over a month, and it removes the temptation to accept dynamic currency conversion at a terminal, which is always the worse rate.
Keep a small emergency fund entirely separate from the trip budget, because the point of it is that you never have to decide whether an unexpected cost is affordable.
tips: No surcharge on eftpos, Mastercard or Visa

faq: How much does it cost to travel Australia in 2026?

The total is driven by distance more than anything else, because fuel and domestic flights are where the money goes. The guide sets out dated Australian dollar benchmarks for transport, accommodation and food, converted into ten currencies.
Is Australia expensive to travel in?

Yes, particularly for accommodation, eating out and covering distance. Camping and self-catering are where it stops being expensive, which is why the gap between a camping trip and a hotel trip is unusually wide here.

sources.label: Reserve Bank of Australia exchange rates

priceTable.note: Illustrative daily totals assembled from the dated component prices in this guide. Long-distance transport, vehicle hire and international flights are separate.

australia-grocery-prices-2026.title: Australia Grocery Prices 2026: Milk $2.45, Eggs $7.19
australia-grocery-prices-2026.description: October 2026 prices: milk $1.60 to $4 a litre, a dozen eggs $4.48 to $10, chicken $9 to $18 a kilo. A solo week of core staples costs about $85.
australia-grocery-prices-2026.imageAlt: Fresh food and groceries at an Australian market
australia-grocery-prices-2026.intro: Community-reported average prices from Numbeo in October 2026 put a litre of milk at $2.45, a 500 g loaf at $3.96, a dozen eggs at $7.19 and a kilo of chicken fillets at $13.14. Self-catering is still the simplest way to control a long travel budget, as long as the basket is planned around a small fridge.

sections.heading: What a road-trip basket needs
body: Build around breakfast, portable lunches and two or three dinners that share ingredients. Oats, bread, eggs, rice or pasta, vegetables and a flexible protein waste less space than a different recipe every night.
Buy small quantities when refrigeration is weak. A cheap bulk pack is expensive if heat, ice melt or a long driving day makes it unsafe.

sections.heading: City prices and remote prices
body: Large supermarkets create more competition and promotional choice. Remote stores and roadhouses may carry fewer sizes at higher prices because transport and stock turnover are different.
Restock before remote legs, but respect interstate biosecurity restrictions on fruit, vegetables, honey, plants and other regulated items.

sections.heading: A realistic weekly figure
body: At Numbeo's community-reported national averages for October 2026, a solo week of core staples comes to about $85: 2 litres of milk, two loaves, a dozen eggs, a kilo of chicken, 500 g of beef, a kilo each of apples, bananas, tomatoes, onions and rice, 2 kg of potatoes, 500 g of cheese and a lettuce. Pantry items, snacks and remote purchases come on top.
Keep a separate allowance for coffee, takeaway and shared meals. Calling every food purchase a grocery hides the choices that are easiest to change.

sections.heading: The supermarket landscape
body: Coles and Woolworths trade across the country, and Aldi is usually cheaper for staples where it trades (CHOICE's June 2026 basket came to $68.60 at Aldi against $77.53 at Woolworths and $78.58 at Coles), but it has no stores in Tasmania or the Northern Territory. IGA and other independents fill the gaps in smaller towns, often at higher prices.
In remote areas the only option is frequently a roadhouse or a community store, where freight and low turnover push prices well above city levels. That is arithmetic rather than gouging.
Do the substantial shop in the last large centre before a remote leg, and buy locally in small towns for the things worth buying there. Both matter: one for your budget, the other for the town.
tips: Aldi is cheapest where it trades
No Aldi in Tasmania or the NT

sections.heading: Shopping for a small fridge in heat
body: Campervan fridges are small and lose efficiency in Australian heat, particularly those running off the vehicle battery. Buy for two or three days rather than a week and keep raw meat sealed at the bottom.

Build meals around a shared set of ingredients so one shop covers the block. Tinned fish, eggs, hard cheese, oats, rice, pasta and root vegetables all survive limited refrigeration and cover a lot of dinners.
A discounted bulk pack is not a saving if half of it is unsafe by day three. In the tropics this is a practical daily consideration rather than a theoretical one.
tips: Buy for three days, not seven
Seal and store raw meat low

sections.heading: Seasonal produce and interstate rules
body: Buying what is in season locally is one of the biggest savings. Mangoes in the north over summer, stone fruit in the southern states, and roadside stalls in growing regions all undercut supermarkets substantially.
Many roadside stalls run on an honesty box and take cash only, though some now accept cards. Carry small notes, because they appear without warning and are often the best produce you will find.

Plan the fridge around quarantine borders and fruit-fly zones. Running produce down before crossing into South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania or the Northern Territory, or into fruit-fly zones such as the Riverland and Sunraysia, avoids buying food twice. Check interstatequarantine.org.au for the current rules.
tips: Buy what is in season locally
Run the fridge down before borders

sections.heading: Saving at the checkout
body: Large supermarkets must show a unit price, such as the price per kilogram or per 100 g, next to the shelf price. Compare that line rather than the pack price, because bigger packs are not always cheaper per kilo.
Many supermarkets mark down fresh bakery and deli items late in the day, so the last shop before closing can be the cheapest one.
Couples and groups save more per person, because one jar, bag or block covers two people for little more than it covers one. Split staples, not just the bill.

faq: How much do groceries cost in Australia?

On Numbeo's community-reported national averages for October 2026, milk is $2.45 a litre, bread $3.96 a loaf, eggs $7.19 a dozen and chicken fillets $13.14 a kilo. A solo week of core staples comes to about $85 before pantry items, and remote stores charge more.
Where is the cheapest place to buy food in Australia?
The major supermarket chains in towns of any size, and Aldi where there is one. The price gap to a remote roadhouse or a small-town store can be large, so stocking up before a long leg usually pays.

sources.label: Numbeo Australia price ranges, updated October 2026

priceTable.note: National community-reported ranges from Numbeo, updated October 2026. Brand, promotion, season, city and remote freight can change the shelf price.

eating-out-australia-prices-2026.title: Eating Out Prices in Australia 2026: Cheap Meals $20 to $45
eating-out-australia-prices-2026.description: A cheap restaurant meal costs $20 to $45 in Sydney, a fast-food combo $15 to $18 and dinner for two $80 to $200 (October 2026). Tipping and surcharges.
eating-out-australia-prices-2026.imageAlt: Outdoor cafe meal in an Australian city
eating-out-australia-prices-2026.intro: A meal at an inexpensive Sydney restaurant costs about $20 to $45 a person, a fast-food combo $15 to $18 and a three-course dinner for two at a mid-range restaurant $80 to $200, on community price data updated in October 2026. These are Sydney figures; the national ones are close (an inexpensive meal runs $17 to $45), but regional and remote prices can differ.

sections.heading: Three workable food styles
body: Self-catering with one purchased coffee or snack keeps the daily total lowest. A mixed day adds one casual meal, while a restaurant-heavy day can exceed the accommodation cost before drinks.
Breakfast and lunch are often easier to control than dinner. Carrying food also prevents a late arrival from becoming an expensive search near a tourist strip.

sections.heading: Read the menu total properly
body: Check whether a weekend or public holiday surcharge applies before ordering. Since 1 October 2026 businesses can no longer surcharge eftpos, Mastercard, Visa, American Express or UnionPay payments, and PayPal surcharges stopped from 5 October 2026, but weekend and public holiday surcharges, booking fees and service fees are not affected. Shared plates, sides and drinks still push an ordinary main well past its headline price.
Remote cafes and small towns have different supply costs and opening hours. Treat a published city range as a benchmark, not an entitlement.

sections.heading: Where eating out earns its place
body: Set a daily food figure and decide in advance how many bought meals it covers. A fixed number of meals out a week is easier to keep than deciding meal by meal at the end of a long drive.
Track the actual amount for a few days. Visitors often remember the main-course price but forget coffee, snacks and delivery fees.

sections.heading: Where the value actually is
body: The bakery, the fish and chip shop and the pub counter meal are three reliable cheap options across the country, and quality in regional towns is often as good as in cities.
Pub meals in particular are an Australian institution and often the only dinner option in a small town. Portions are large and prices are often cheaper than a city restaurant.

Cafes generally stop serving food earlier than visitors expect, and small towns can have nothing open after about eight. Carrying something you can cook is what stops a late arrival becoming a missed dinner.
tips: Pub counter meals are good value

sections.heading: Surcharges and payment
body: Public holiday and weekend surcharges are legal and common, and a cafe or restaurant has to show them on the menu. Card surcharges on eftpos, Mastercard, Visa, American Express and UnionPay ended on 1 October 2026, so the menu price plus any weekend or public holiday surcharge, booking fee or service fee is what you pay.
Tipping is not expected in Australia and staff are paid an award wage. Some payment terminals now prompt for a tip, which is a recent import rather than a local norm.
Cash is increasingly rare and many venues are card only, but remote roadhouses and honesty boxes still need it. Carry a small amount even if you rarely use it.
tips: Keep some cash for remote areas

sections.heading: Eating well without eating out constantly
body: Spend deliberately on food tied to the place: seafood on the coast, mangoes in the tropics in season, a winery lunch in the Barossa or Margaret River. These are the meals people remember.
Use simple groceries on transfer days, when you are arriving late and leaving early and a meal is fuel rather than an experience. That pattern buys the good meals without making every day expensive.
Lunch menus at good restaurants deliver most of the dinner experience for less. If you want one memorable meal in an expensive town, book it at lunchtime.
tips: Spend on food tied to the region

sections.heading: Ordering and portion expectations
body: Australian portions are generous and a main course is usually enough without sides. Entrees are starters rather than mains, which confuses North American visitors regularly, and sharing a starter is normal.

Bring-your-own alcohol is common at unlicensed restaurants and some licensed ones, usually with a corkage fee per bottle or per person, so check when booking. It can substantially reduce the cost of a meal out.
Ask locals rather than searching, particularly in small towns where the best meal is frequently at a bowls club or a pub with no online presence at all.

faq: How much is a meal out in Australia?

An inexpensive restaurant meal costs about $20 to $45 a person in Sydney and a fast-food combo $15 to $18, on October 2026 community price data. A three-course dinner for two at a mid-range restaurant runs $80 to $200 before drinks.
Do you tip in Australia?

No. Tipping is not expected and restaurant staff are paid award wages, though rounding up or leaving something for exceptional service is welcome. Sunday and public holiday surcharges are normal and legal when the menu shows them.

sources.label: Reserve Bank of Australia: card surcharge ban FAQs

priceTable.note: Sydney community-contributed ranges updated October 2026. Waterfronts, resorts, airports, events and table service can cost more.

alcohol-coffee-drink-prices-australia.title: Beer & Coffee Prices in Australia 2026: Pub Beer $7 to $16
alcohol-coffee-drink-prices-australia.description: A pub beer costs $7 to $16 and a cappuccino $4.50 to $8 in Sydney (October 2026). Bottle-shop beer and wine prices, and how to keep drinks cheap.
alcohol-coffee-drink-prices-australia.imageAlt: Australian cafe drinks on a table
alcohol-coffee-drink-prices-australia.intro: A 500 ml draught beer in a Sydney pub costs about $7 to $16 and a cappuccino $4.50 to $8, on community price data updated in October 2026, while a 500 ml bottle of beer from a bottle shop runs about $3.50 to $12 nationally. Drinks add up one round at a time.

sections.heading: Retail and venue prices are different products
body: A pub price includes the venue, staff and service rather than only the liquid. Compare like with like and do not describe a bottle-shop equivalent as the price of a poured drink.
Happy hours and promotions are temporary. Build the budget from the ordinary range, then treat a discount as margin.

sections.heading: Wine at the bottle shop and at the bar
body: A mid-range 750 ml bottle of wine costs about $12 to $30 from a bottle shop, and it pours roughly five 150 ml glasses. Ordered by the glass in a bar or restaurant, the same wine usually costs considerably more per serve, so a bottle shared at camp is where wine is cheapest.
Some restaurants, mostly unlicensed ones, let you bring your own bottle for a corkage fee, which turns a bottle-shop price into dinner wine. Ask about it when you book rather than at the table.

sections.heading: Control the quiet daily total
body: Two coffees and two venue drinks each day can become a substantial weekly amount. Decide which stops matter rather than buying by habit.
Keep drinking water accessible and refill only from potable taps. In hot conditions, hydration and shade belong in the safety plan, not the entertainment budget.

sections.heading: Coffee is a daily line
body: Australian coffee culture is strong and the standard in regional towns is genuinely high, which is precisely why it becomes a budget item. Two flat whites a day for two people accumulates without ever feeling like a decision.
A stovetop pot or an AeroPress in the van covers the morning cup for a fraction of the cafe price and leaves the cafe stop as something chosen rather than automatic.
Roadhouse coffee on long drives is variable at best. On outback routes, making your own is usually both cheaper and considerably better.
tips: Two cups a day adds up fast

sections.heading: Buying alcohol in Australia
body: Packaged alcohol is mostly sold through licensed bottle shops, often next to a supermarket but operating separately, though Aldi and some independent grocers sell it in-store. Trading hours are regulated and vary by state.

Alcohol restrictions apply across many communities and regions, particularly in the Northern Territory, parts of Queensland, Western Australia and South Australia. Carrying alcohol into a restricted area carries substantial penalties.
Check before travelling with alcohol into remote areas. The restrictions are legally enforced, apply to visitors as much as residents, and ignorance is not a defence.

sections.heading: Drinking and the driving day
body: The general limit is 0.05 for full licence holders, zero for learner and provisional drivers, and zero or 0.02 for many professional drivers depending on the state (0.02 in NSW). Random breath testing is common, including on rural roads and during the day.
On a road trip the only safe approach is to separate drinking from driving completely: stay where you are drinking, use a designated driver, or drink once the vehicle is parked for the night.

Morning-after driving catches people out. The body takes at least an hour to clear each standard drink, often longer, and coffee or a shower does not speed it up, so a heavy evening can leave you over the limit well into the next morning.
tips: 0.05 general, zero for learners and provisionals
Random testing is common and daytime

sections.heading: Water is the one to get right
body: Tap water is safe and good across almost all Australian towns and cities, and buying bottled water is close to pure waste. Carry refillable bottles and fill at any potable tap in a town, campground or public facility.

In remote and bush settings the position reverses: bore water may be mineralised or unsuitable, tank water is untreated, and surface water in agricultural country can carry chemical contamination. Treat anything that is not a marked potable town supply.
Carry a decent insulated bottle so cold water is always on hand in the heat; it costs nothing to refill.

faq: How much is a beer in Australia?

A 500 ml draught beer in a Sydney pub costs about $7.15 to $16 on October 2026 community price data, and a 500 ml bottle from a bottle shop about $3.50 to $12 nationally. Buying from a bottle shop rather than a bar is one of the biggest savings on a long trip.
How much does coffee cost in Australia?

A regular cappuccino costs about $4.50 to $8 in Sydney and $4 to $8 nationally on October 2026 community price data, with inner-city cafes often at the top of the range. Two coffees a day for two people becomes a real budget line on a long trip.

sources.label: NHMRC: how long alcohol takes to clear
Northern Territory: buying and drinking alcohol

priceTable.note: Community-contributed Australia and Sydney ranges updated October 2026. Serving size, venue, promotion and location vary.

accommodation-costs-australia-2026.title: Accommodation costs in Australia: hostels, hotels and comfortable stays
accommodation-costs-australia-2026.description: Realistic price bands from a dorm bed to a boutique hotel, plus the dates and extras that change the total.
accommodation-costs-australia-2026.intro: The room is often the largest fixed cost of an Australian trip. Tourism Australia’s planning benchmarks show an enormous ladder, from simple shared accommodation to premium resorts.

sections.heading: Compare the total stay
body: A lower room rate can lose its advantage after parking, linen, breakfast, booking fees or a distant location. Compare the final amount for the same number of people and nights.
A private room priced per person and a hotel priced per room are not directly comparable until occupancy is included.

sections.heading: Peak dates change everything
body: School holidays, festivals, sporting events and dry-season demand can multiply rates. Coastal summer weekends and small gateway towns deserve early checks.
Use refundable terms where uncertainty is real, then record the cancellation deadline beside the trip stop.

sections.heading: Mix accommodation types
body: A full-service room after several camping nights can solve laundry, charging, weather and rest in one purchase. It can be better value than forcing an unsuitable cheap night.
Reserve premium spending for places where the property itself adds to the experience rather than using it automatically on transfer nights.

sections.heading: What each type is actually for
body: A hostel dorm is the cheapest bed and buys a kitchen and company. A caravan park cabin costs more than a site and less than a motel and solves a wet or hot night. A motel is the standard regional middle option.
Pub accommodation in country towns is frequently the best value in Australia, offering a simple room above a bar with a good counter meal downstairs for well below motel rates.
Station stays and farm stays are a distinctive option in remote areas and often the only accommodation for hundreds of kilometres. Most take cash and few have reliable online booking.
tips: Country pubs are often best value
Cabins solve a hot or wet night

sections.heading: When paying for a room is right
body: After several nights of free camping, before a very early flight or ferry, when someone is unwell, or when heat makes a tent genuinely unsafe. In each case the room keeps the trip going rather than being a luxury.

A room also resets everything at once: laundry, hot water, charging, air conditioning and a proper night's sleep. Counted against the jobs it replaces it is frequently better value than the nightly rate suggests.
Budget for a few of these in advance so the decision is easy rather than an argument. Trips that assume every night will be free have no room for the day that goes wrong.
tips: Heat can make a tent unsafe
A room resets the whole vehicle
Budget for a few in advance

sections.heading: Peak season and booking windows
body: School holidays, Easter and Christmas fill coastal accommodation across the country, with minimum stays and substantially higher rates. The northern dry season does the same to Broome, Exmouth, Darwin and Cairns.
Book direct rather than through a platform where you can. It is frequently cheaper and gives you a person to talk to about a late arrival or a site that fits your vehicle.
Longer stays attract weekly rates at many caravan parks, sometimes a substantial discount. If you are basing somewhere for four nights or more, ask rather than booking night by night.

sections.heading: Reading the total rather than the rate
body: Compare the final amount for your actual party and nights, including linen, parking, booking fees and whether breakfast is included. A per-person rate and a per-room rate look similar and diverge sharply with every extra person.

Check the location as well as the price. A cheaper place twenty minutes out of town costs fuel twice and removes the option of walking to dinner, which is frequently the reason you wanted a room in the first place.
Where a town is expensive, look twenty minutes out. Regional accommodation drops sharply just outside the tourist centre and the drive is usually trivial.
tips: Linen and parking are often extra
Location can cost more than the rate

faq: How much is accommodation in Australia per night?

It runs from a hostel dorm through a caravan park cabin and a motel to a hotel room, and the guide prices each with dated figures. Coastal Queensland and Sydney over summer sit well above the national picture.
What is the cheapest way to sleep in Australia?
Camping, by a wide margin, and a council or national park site costs a fraction of a hostel dorm. The saving holds only if the vehicle and fuel to reach those sites are already part of the plan.

sources.label: Reserve Bank of Australia exchange rates

priceTable.note: Tourism Australia planning benchmarks. These are indicative starting prices, not live quotes for every date.

camping-fees-australia-2026.title: Camping Fees Australia 2026: National Park Prices by State
camping-fees-australia-2026.description: National park camping in 2026: $7.75 a person in Queensland, $10 to $20 an adult in WA and the NT, from $16 a site in Victoria, plus entry fees.
camping-fees-australia-2026.imageAlt: Caravan and tent at an Australian campground
camping-fees-australia-2026.intro: Australian national park camping in 2026 runs from free to more than $40 a night at the busiest serviced sites, such as Tidal River at Wilsons Promontory: Queensland charges $7.75 per person, Western Australia and the Northern Territory $10 to $20 per adult, Victoria's half-price bookable campgrounds start at $16 a site, and some NSW campgrounds charge nothing beyond a $6 booking fee. Park entry, passes and whether the fee is per person or per site change the total more than the headline rate.

sections.heading: National park fees by state
body: There is no national parks pass. Every state runs its own booking system, fee scale and pass, and a pass bought in one state is no use in the next.

Entry and camping are charged separately in several states, so a cheap nightly rate can cost more once entry is added. Tasmania needs a Parks Pass for every national park, while South Australia waives vehicle entry with most campground bookings.

sections.heading: Per person or per site: a worked example
body: Take two adults and two children aged 8 and 10 for three nights. A Queensland national park campsite costs $93 at the $31 family rate, a Western Australian campground with basic facilities costs $120 ($15 per adult and $5 per child each night), and a Northern Territory Category A campground costs $114 at the $38 family rate.

A Victorian bookable site from $16 a night comes to about $48 for the same three nights, because Victoria charges per site rather than per person. The order flips for a solo traveller, who pays $23.25 in Queensland and $45 at the same WA campground.
Run the numbers for your own group and nights, then add entry, power and booking fees. A powered site with showers can be better value than a cheaper bush camp once you count what it replaces.
tips: Count your group, not the headline

sections.heading: Holiday parks and caravan parks
body: Commercial holiday parks and caravan parks set their own prices, usually per site for a stated number of people, with extra charges for more guests, power and peak dates. Check the park's own rate page and its minimum-stay rules for school holidays and long weekends.

Advertised specials often need a minimum stay or limited dates, so record them as offers rather than normal rates. In AussieCamps, holiday parks listed by the BookEasy booking partner can be browsed and booked without the Pass.
tips: Prices are per site for set guests

sections.heading: Use paid and simple nights deliberately
body: A low-facility night works when the vehicle and supplies are ready. A serviced night earns its price when tanks, batteries, laundry and people all need a reset.
Keep a paid, legal alternative saved near popular free or low-cost areas, so a full site or a changed local rule never forces an unsafe late drive.

sections.heading: Free camping and what it really costs
body: Free camping saves real money when the vehicle is set up for it and the route already passes legal sites. It stops saving when you drive an extra sixty kilometres to reach one.
The hidden costs are showers, laundry, water, dump points and the paid nights that self-sufficiency still needs. Budget for a paid night more often than you plan to take one.
A single council fine for camping where it is banned can cancel weeks of savings, so free is only free where the land manager allows it.
tips: Do not drive far to save a fee
One fine cancels weeks of saving

sections.heading: Booking fees, refunds and extras
body: NSW National Parks adds a non-refundable booking fee to every campground booking, and $6 at campgrounds with no camping fee. Cancelling 31 days or more ahead refunds 75% of the camping fee, and later cancellations 50%.

Victoria lets one booking hold up to three sites in the same campground, and every site you can drive to includes one vehicle in the fee. Tasmania moves to a new Parks Online Booking System on 3 November 2026, with higher fees at campgrounds such as Fortescue Bay and Mount Field.
Extra vehicles, trailers and visitors can each add a charge. Read the booking page for what the fee covers before you pay.
tips: Victoria: up to three sites a booking

sections.heading: Booking systems differ by state
body: Queensland and South Australia open park bookings 12 months ahead, Western Australia's Park Stay WA 180 days ahead, and Victoria releases sites in quarterly batches. Learn the system for each state on your route before you need it.
The busiest sites go fast. Ningaloo Coast campgrounds release a month at a time on the first Tuesday at 10am Perth time, so mark the release date when a particular site matters.
Keep booking confirmations on your phone, because the campgrounds with the weakest reception are often the ones where a ranger asks to see one.
tips: Mark release dates for busy sites

faq: How much does camping cost per night in Australia?

In national parks, from nothing to more than $40 a night at the busiest serviced sites in 2026: Queensland charges $7.75 per person, WA and the NT $10 to $20 per adult, Victoria's half-price bookable campgrounds start at $16 a site, and some NSW campgrounds charge only a $6 booking fee. Commercial holiday parks set their own prices.
Do you pay park entry on top of camping fees?

In some states. Tasmania requires a Parks Pass for every national park, WA charges $17 a vehicle at parks such as Karijini, 45 NSW parks charge vehicle entry, and NT visitors need a Parks Visitor Pass. South Australia waives entry with most campground bookings, and Queensland has no general park entry fee, but driving on K'gari and the other sand islands needs a paid vehicle access permit.

australia-road-trip-fuel-cost-2026.title: Australian road-trip fuel costs in 2026
australia-road-trip-fuel-cost-2026.description: Calculate petrol or diesel from distance and consumption, using current official city benchmarks and a remote-road margin.
australia-road-trip-fuel-cost-2026.imageAlt: Vehicle refuelling during an Australian road trip
australia-road-trip-fuel-cost-2026.intro: Fuel is where distance becomes money. Official Fuel Plan data for 5 August 2026 put the five-largest-city average at A$2.08 per litre for petrol and A$2.47 for diesel, while remote prices can be materially higher.

sections.heading: The calculation
body: Multiply kilometres by litres per 100 kilometres, divide by 100, then multiply by the price per litre. A 1,000 km drive at 12 L/100 km uses 120 litres.
Use the vehicle’s real loaded consumption when possible. Roof loads, towing, wind, speed, terrain and air conditioning can move it beyond the brochure figure.

sections.heading: Capital averages are not remote quotes
body: The official city benchmark is a transparent starting point. Remote roadhouses carry different costs and are too important to skip merely to chase a lower price farther ahead.
Fill conservatively, know the next dependable service and keep fuel stops inside the trip plan.
tips: Never run the tank to empty

sections.heading: Reduce cost without reducing safety
body: Slower, smoother driving and correct tyre pressures can help, but pressures must suit the vehicle, load and manufacturer guidance. Never coast unsafely or carry fuel in an unsuitable container.
The biggest saving is often fewer unnecessary kilometres. Group nearby stops and avoid crossing the same city or remote section repeatedly.

sections.heading: Where fuel costs most
body: Prices are lowest in the capitals and highest at remote roadhouses, where the premium can be very large. The Nullarbor, the Kimberley, central Australia and the Cape all carry substantial mark-ups.
That premium is never a reason to stretch a tank. The cost of twenty extra litres at a high price is trivial compared with running dry hundreds of kilometres from anywhere with no reception.
Fuel price apps and supermarket discount vouchers save real money in urban and regional areas and are largely irrelevant once remote, where there is no competing station.
tips: Never stretch a tank to save money
Fuel apps help in town only

sections.heading: What actually changes consumption
body: Load, roof boxes, headwind, sustained climbing, towing and speed all matter, and a loaded campervan into a headwind can use a quarter more than the brochure figure. Air conditioning has a modest effect by comparison.
Tyre pressures should be set for the loaded vehicle rather than the empty one. Rental campervans frequently arrive underinflated, which costs fuel and handling at the same time.
Every ten kilometres per hour above about ninety costs noticeably more in a high-sided vehicle. On long straights, slowing down saves fuel and reduces fatigue together.
tips: Set pressures for the loaded vehicle
Speed costs more in tall vehicles

sections.heading: Carrying fuel and the remote legs
body: Where the gap between stations exceeds your range, carry additional fuel in approved jerry cans, properly secured and vented, and never inside the living space of a vehicle.

Work out your genuine range from measured consumption rather than the manufacturer's figure, then plan to arrive with a substantial reserve. Roadhouses can be closed, out of stock or unable to process a card.
Diesel is generally more available than premium unleaded in remote Australia, which is a practical argument for diesel on outback routes independent of the fuel price itself.
tips: Approved jerry cans, secured and vented

sections.heading: Fuel quality and vehicle requirements
body: Premium unleaded is not available at every remote roadhouse, and some carry only regular unleaded and diesel. If your vehicle requires premium, check availability along the route rather than assuming.

Diesel in remote areas is generally reliable and widely stocked because it is what the trucks and stations use. That availability, rather than the pump price, is the strongest practical argument for diesel on outback routes.
Record the odometer at each fill even if you do nothing else, because it gives you a real range figure within a week and removes most fuel anxiety.

faq: How much does fuel cost in Australia?

The guide gives dated prices per litre for petrol and diesel and works them through real routes. Remote roadhouse prices run far above city prices, sometimes by half again, which is what breaks outback budgets.
How do you estimate fuel for an Australian road trip?

Take the route distance and add a fifth for detours, multiply by your vehicle's real consumption in litres per 100 km and divide by 100 to get litres, then multiply by the price per litre. So a van using 12 litres per 100 km needs about 120 litres for every 1,000 km driven. Use real consumption, not the brochure figure: a loaded van into a headwind will not meet its rated economy.

public-transport-costs-australia-2026.title: Australian Public Transport Costs 2026: Fares From 50c
public-transport-costs-australia-2026.description: Queensland fares are a flat 50c, Perth's DayRider $7, Melbourne's daily cap $5.70 until 1 January 2027 and Sydney's $19.30 Mon to Thu. Airport fees too.
public-transport-costs-australia-2026.imageAlt: Public transport in an Australian city
public-transport-costs-australia-2026.intro: Queensland charges a flat 50 cents a trip, Perth caps a day at $7, Melbourne's full-fare daily cap is $5.70 under half-price fares that run until 1 January 2027, and Sydney caps adult Opal travel at $19.30 a day from Monday to Thursday. Each city counts differently, so compare a whole day of travel rather than one ticket.

sections.heading: Compare the same unit
body: A fare per journey is not a daily maximum. Count the expected trips, understand transfers and then apply the operator’s current cap rules.
Use the accepted payment method correctly. Contactless, stored-value and cash fares can differ, and tapping errors can remove a cap or create an incomplete trip.

sections.heading: Airport travel is often separate
body: Airport rail often sits outside ordinary fares. Brisbane's Airtrain is excluded from Queensland's 50-cent fare, and Sydney's airport stations add a station access fee on top of the rail fare, with its own weekly cap.
Price the airport leg separately before deciding whether rail, bus, shuttle, taxi or rideshare works best.

sections.heading: Use transport to avoid city driving
body: Parking, tolls and unfamiliar traffic can make public transport valuable even when several people share a car. Compare the full vehicle cost, not only the train fare.
Leave the campervan or caravan at a legal base where possible and use city transport for dense central areas.

sections.heading: Each city has its own card
body: Australia has no national transport card. Sydney uses Opal, Melbourne myki, south-east Queensland the go card, Perth SmartRider and Adelaide metroCARD, and contactless bank cards now work on many of these networks.

Melbourne accepts contactless Visa and Mastercard on trains, trams and myki-enabled buses, with the bus rollout completed by 26 July 2026. Since 13 October 2026 concession holders can also tap a bank card once they link their concession entitlement online, but Youth myki holders still need a myki, so check the current rules before relying on a bank card.

Daily and weekly caps exist in most systems and change the arithmetic substantially once you make several trips. Work out the expected number of journeys before choosing between a pass and paying per trip.
tips: Melbourne: bank cards on trains, trams and buses

sections.heading: Airport connections
body: Sydney's airport stations charge a station access fee of $18.61 per adult trip on top of the rail fare, capped at $37.75 a week, so the airport train costs far more than an ordinary trip. Brisbane's Airtrain is priced as a separate service.
Perth's Airport line trains run at ordinary Transperth fares. Because it is a normal fare, a rideshare only competes for larger groups with luggage, so price both.

Sydney's station access fee sits outside the Opal daily and weekly caps and Brisbane's Airtrain sits outside the 50-cent fare, but Perth's Airport line is covered by ordinary Transperth fares and DayRider. Price the airport leg separately when comparing options.
tips: Sydney adds a station access fee
Sydney and Brisbane airport rail is priced separately
Rideshare can beat fares for groups

sections.heading: When to leave the vehicle behind
body: Driving a campervan into central Sydney or Melbourne is unpleasant, parking is expensive and height restrictions catch large vehicles out constantly. Leaving it at a caravan park and taking transport in is faster and cheaper.
The same applies in most capitals. Base yourself outside the centre and use the local network for the days you want to be in the city.
Outside the capitals and a handful of regional centres, public transport is minimal to non-existent. A trip planned around buses works between cities and does not reach campsites or trailheads.
tips: Height limits catch vans in city car parks

sections.heading: Concessions and visitor passes
body: Concession fares generally require an Australian-issued concession entitlement, and overseas student or senior cards are usually not accepted. Budget for full adult fares unless you have confirmed otherwise for that specific network.

Some cities sell visitor passes bundling transport with attractions. Work out the number of trips and entries you will actually use before buying, because these usually assume a busier itinerary than most travellers keep.

In Perth, travel on Sundays is free with a SmartRider or a contactless card, and under-18s ride free in Victoria with a Youth myki (contactless bank cards cannot be used for Youth travel). For a stay of more than a few days, check whether the city has a weekly cap (Sydney's is $50) before paying day by day.
tips: Visitor passes assume a busy schedule

faq: Can you travel Australia without a car?
Between the capitals, yes. Beyond them the network thins fast, and many of the coastal and outback places most people come for are hard to reach without a vehicle or a tour.
How much does public transport cost in Australian cities?

Queensland charges a flat 50 cents a trip, Perth caps a day at $7 and Sundays are free with a SmartRider or bank card, Melbourne's daily cap is $5.70 until 1 January 2027, and Sydney's adult Opal cap is $19.30 Monday to Thursday and $9.65 Friday to Sunday and on public holidays.

Transport for NSW: getting to and from Sydney Airport
Victorian Government: tap and go rolling out on buses
Victorian Government: tap and go for concession passengers
