sections.heading: 1. AussieCamps: plan where you will stop and sleep
body: AussieCamps treats a trip as a list of places rather than a line on a map. You add campgrounds, caravan parks, rest areas or any saved place as stops, put them in order, and see the driving distance and time for each leg and for the whole journey. Each stop can carry an arrival date, and the app shows the forecast for arrival dates within the forecast range, which is the detail that changes plans most often in Australia.

Around the route it keeps a trip checklist and packing list, notes, a cover photo, and visited progress as you go. A trip can be shared or synced to your calendar with its stops and dates. Because the place directory lives on the phone, details for every stop stay readable out of signal, while the map, directions and forecasts need a connection. When it is time to drive, directions open in Apple Maps or Google Maps.

The download is free, as are bookable hotels, motels, B&Bs, holiday parks and tours from BookEasy. Trips, collections and the campground, rest area and dump point data need the AussieCamps Pass, sold as a weekly subscription or a one-off lifetime purchase, with in-app purchases listed at A$2.99 to A$9.99 on the Australian App Store.
Choose something else if you need turn-by-turn navigation inside the planner, if you are on Android, or if your trip is mostly cities, where a general itinerary app fits better.
tips: Stops, dates and forecasts in one plan
Navigation hands off to Apple or Google Maps

sections.heading: 2. Google Maps: the navigator most people already have
body: Google Maps is free, covers Australia well and gives live traffic and turn-by-turn directions. For planning, it allows up to 9 stops on a route, counting the final destination, which is enough for a day's drive but not for a two-week loop, so long trips end up split across several routes or saved lists.

Download the areas you will drive through before you leave. Google's help pages say offline driving directions work only when the whole route is inside a downloaded area, offline maps expire unless updated, and traffic is not available offline.

sections.heading: 3. Apple Maps: the iPhone default, with more stops
body: Apple Maps is built into every iPhone and its support guide allows a multi-stop driving route with up to 14 stops, which goes further than Google Maps for a single route. Offline maps can be downloaded, and Apple says they support turn-by-turn driving directions without a connection.

Apple notes that offline maps are not available in every country or region, so download a test area before you rely on it. Like Google Maps, it plans the drive rather than the nights: it will not tell you which rest areas allow an overnight stop.

sections.heading: 4. Wanderlog: an itinerary builder for mixed trips
body: Wanderlog is a general travel planner with a 4.9 rating from more than 5,000 Australian ratings. Its App Store listing says you can add unlimited stops for free and see times and distances between places, which suits a trip that mixes drives with days in Sydney or Melbourne and flights between.

Its help centre, though not its store listing, lists offline access to trip plans and route optimisation as Pro features. The Australian App Store lists several Pro prices, from A$50.99 to A$99.99 a year and A$25.99 a month, so check the price shown to you. It has no dedicated camping or rest area directory and no in-app navigation.

sections.heading: 5. WikiCamps Australia: trip planning inside a camping app
body: WikiCamps includes a Trip Planner: you create a trip, add sections such as regions or days, then places and notes, and drag a progress bar as you travel. Enter your vehicle's fuel use and a price per litre and it estimates fuel use and cost between the places in your trip.

It costs A$9.99 once per platform, and up to three planned trips can be downloaded for use without signal. Its help pages do not mention drive times per leg, so pair it with a navigation app for timings.

sections.heading: 6. ExplorOz Traveller: route planning off the bitumen
body: For outback and 4WD trips, ExplorOz Traveller plans and navigates on its own EOTopo topographic map, which shows named roads and 4WD tracks, with track access notes. With EOTopo access downloaded, it works across Australia with no signal.

The app is A$59.99, and offline use needs EOTopo at A$59.99 a year, the 2026 edition at A$79.99 for four years, or Pro Access at A$99.99 a year. That is far more than a sealed-road trip needs, and exactly what a Simpson Desert crossing does.
tips: Offline topo map with EOTopo access

sections.heading: Also worth knowing
body: TripIt organises bookings rather than routes: forward confirmation emails and it builds an itinerary with flights, hire cars and accommodation, available offline. Polarsteps plans and then tracks your route automatically, which suits travellers who want a record of the trip as much as a plan.
We left out Roadtrippers, a popular planner in North America, because its App Store listing says it is designed for road trips in the USA and Canada only.
tips: Roadtrippers is USA and Canada only

sections.heading: How we compared them
body: Each app's price, in-app purchases, rating and limits were checked on the Australian App Store and in the developer's own help pages on 20 October 2026. Stop limits are the ones the developers publish. We looked at what matters on an Australian road trip: how far apart the stops are, whether you can see where to sleep, and what still works out of signal.
Our own app earns its money from the Pass, and none of the others paid for a place here. Tell us through the support page if anything has changed.

faq: What is the best app to plan a road trip in Australia?

Use two kinds of app. A planner such as AussieCamps decides the stops, nights and dates, with distance and drive time for each leg, and a navigation app such as Google Maps or Apple Maps handles the drive itself. For remote 4WD tracks, ExplorOz Traveller does both on its own maps.
How many stops can you add in Google Maps?

Up to 9 stops on one route, counting the final destination, according to Google's help pages. Apple Maps allows up to 14 stops on a driving route. Longer trips need splitting into several routes or a dedicated trip planner.
Does Roadtrippers work in Australia?
Its App Store listing says it is designed for road trips in the USA and Canada only, so it is not a good fit for Australia.
Can I plan a road trip offline in Australia?

Partly. Google Maps and Apple Maps can navigate within downloaded areas, AussieCamps keeps place details on the phone with the Pass, and WikiCamps keeps up to three downloaded trips. Live traffic, forecasts and new routes still need signal in most apps.

That matters for free camping because the rules sit with the land manager: those places are different things, and the app keeps campgrounds, national parks and roadside rest areas as separate categories, with each place's fees listed. It is first here because free camps tend to be where the signal is weakest, and its place details are stored on the phone with no region to download. The map, directions and weather still need a connection.

It is not free to use for camping. The download, map and search are free, as are bookable hotels, motels, holiday parks and tours from BookEasy, but campgrounds, rest areas, dump points and water need the AussieCamps Pass, a weekly subscription or one-off lifetime purchase with in-app purchases from A$2.99 to A$9.99. sections.heading: 2. CamperMate: free, with no in-app purchases
body: CamperMate is free with no in-app purchases on the Australian App Store and lists free camps alongside holiday parks, dump stations and toilets across Australia and New Zealand. Travellers add reviews and photos and suggest places, alongside partner listings, and maps and key information can be downloaded for use without signal.
It is supported by advertising, bookings and deals, so paid options appear next to free ones. For a traveller who wants to spend nothing on apps, it is a good first install.

sections.heading: 3. Full Range Camping: a free directory with a Free Camps category
body: Full Range Camping, formerly FreeRange Camping, keeps its directory of camping spots and businesses free to browse and has a Free Camps category. Its app uses online maps unless you have Premium, which adds offline caching, weather radar and member discounts.
Premium is listed on the App Store at A$49.99 a year or A$99.99 for life, but when we checked, the company's website said new Premium memberships were unavailable while its app mapping is updated.

sections.heading: 4. WikiCamps Australia: not free, but the free camps are well reviewed

Offline use needs the main Australia content downloaded first, with up to three planned trips saved for use without signal.

sections.heading: 5. CAMPS Australia Wide: low cost, checked sites
body: CAMPS lists more than 16,000 campsites that Camps Australia Wide says its team has checked in person, with no paid listings. It is free for 7 days and then A$14.99 a year; the company retired its free app access in December 2024, so there is no free tier after the trial.

sections.heading: 6. Free government tools from the land managers

Free does not always mean no booking. In Queensland, every camp in a national park, state forest or recreation area needs a paid permit booked before arrival. Almost all of Victoria's state forest campgrounds are free and cannot be booked, and Main Roads WA allows stays of up to 24 hours only at its rest areas signed for it. faq: What is the best free camping app in Australia?

If the app itself must cost nothing, CamperMate is free with no in-app purchases and lists free camps among its places. AussieCamps is free to download but needs the Pass for its official campground and rest area data, and WikiCamps costs A$9.99 once per platform.
Is there a free app for free camps in Australia?

Yes. CamperMate is free, and Full Range Camping's directory, including its Free Camps category, is free to browse. Government park and forest agencies also publish their campgrounds for free, though many of those sites charge a camping fee.
Do free campsites still need booking?

Sometimes. Queensland needs a paid permit for every camp in its parks and forests, NSW National Parks charges a booking fee even where camping is free, and almost all Victorian state forest campgrounds are free and cannot be booked. Check the land manager for each site.
Can you sleep at rest areas in Australia?

Only where the road authority or sign allows it. Queensland lets vehicles stop at rest areas for up to 20 hours unless signed otherwise, and Main Roads WA allows up to 24 hours only at rest areas signed for it. Read the sign before you stay.

best-caravan-rv-apps-australia.imageAlt: Caravans and motorhomes parked at a coastal campground near Jurien Bay, Western Australia
best-caravan-rv-apps-australia.intro: Travelling with a caravan or motorhome changes what you need from an app: whether a site takes your rig, where the next dump point and drinking water are, and where you can pull over for the night. No single app answers all of it. We make AussieCamps, so we have put it first, and each section says when another app fits your rig better. Prices and ratings were checked on the Australian App Store on 20 October 2026.

sections.heading: 1. AussieCamps: official data for the stops a caravan needs
body: AussieCamps draws its campgrounds, rest areas, dump points and drinking water from state park agencies, road authorities and public facility datasets. For a caravan or motorhome that means 1,393 dump points, 230 of them with a washout, 3,004 drinking water points, 5,552 rest areas and 1,838 campgrounds. Place pages list the features the source records, such as caravan sites, powered sites or a heavy vehicle area at a rest area, along with access notes from the park agency such as 2WD or high-clearance 4WD, and you can filter by those features and by cost.

Trips work as a list of stops with the distance and drive time for each leg, a forecast for each arrival date within the forecast range, and a checklist for the jobs before you hitch up. Place details are stored on the phone, so they stay readable out of signal, while the map, directions and weather need a connection.

The download is free, and so are bookable holiday parks, motels and tours from BookEasy. Everything else, including campgrounds, rest areas, dump points, water and trips, needs the AussieCamps Pass, a weekly subscription or one-off lifetime purchase, with in-app purchases listed at A$2.99 to A$9.99.

Choose another app if you need a big rig filter: AussieCamps shows a vehicle detail only where the source records one, so it cannot tell you whether every campground fits a long van. It is iPhone only and has no traveller reviews.

sections.heading: 2. CAMPS Australia Wide: the pick for big rigs
body: If your main question is whether a site takes your rig, CAMPS is the strongest choice here. Its App Store listing lets you filter by camping set-up, including caravan, motorhome, camper trailer, RV and big rig, and lists vehicle suitability as a site detail. Its dump point symbols show big rig access and the fee. The company says its team has visited sites since 1992, lists more than 16,000 of them and takes no paid listings.

The first 7 days are free, then it costs A$14.99 a year, and maps with all site information can be downloaded for use without signal. It is rated 4.4 from 3,476 Australian ratings. Camps also runs Rig Ready, a free towing weight checker on its website.
tips: Sites checked by its own team

sections.heading: 3. WikiCamps Australia: what other caravanners say
body: WikiCamps costs A$9.99 once per platform and is rated 4.5 from 16,663 Australian ratings. It lists more than 65,000 sites and 1.3 million reviews by its own count, all contributed by users, which is where you learn whether a turn is tight or a site is too sloping for a van. Its filters include site features for access by people, pets and vehicles, and its Trip Planner estimates fuel cost between stops.

Maps and up to three planned trips can be downloaded for use without signal. The developer has added a small number of ads in the reviews, fees and photos sections. Vehicle access is recorded by users, so check a site's access features and reviews before you take a long van in.
tips: Some ads in a paid app

sections.heading: 4. CMCA Traveller: for motorhome club members
body: The Campervan and Motorhome Club of Australia gives its members CMCA Traveller, which lists more than 200,000 points of interest by its own count, including campgrounds, caravan parks, RV parks and dump points, with route planning, voice-guided navigation and maps you can download before you lose signal. It is free to download but works only for members, after a 14-day free trial.

Membership costs A$60 a year for motorhome, campervan, fifth-wheeler and bus owners, or A$55 a year as an associate with a caravan or camper trailer, with the digital magazine. CMCA also runs the RV Friendly program: towns that offer short-term, low-cost overnight parking of 24 or 48 hours for self-contained vehicles, drinking water and a free dump point. The app has only 25 Australian ratings, averaging 3.2.
tips: RV Friendly towns from the same club

sections.heading: 5. CamperMate: free, and made for hire campervans
body: CamperMate is free with no in-app purchases on the Australian App Store and lists holiday parks, free camps, dump stations, toilets and supermarkets across Australia and New Zealand. Maps and key information can be downloaded for use without signal, and it is the official travel partner of hire companies Apollo, Maui, Britz and Mighty Camper.
It suits a hired campervan well. For a large caravan, note that its listing documents no filter for vehicle size, so check each site's details or reviews before you commit to a narrow track.

sections.heading: 6. Sygic GPS Truck & Caravan: navigation that knows your size
body: Sygic plans routes by vehicle type, size and weight, aiming to avoid low bridges and narrow streets, and its maps can be downloaded for use without signal. It is rated 4.4 from 1,766 Australian ratings. The app is free to download, and its Camper Australia in-app purchase is listed at A$79.99.
It is a navigation app, not a directory: pair it with one of the apps above to decide where to stop.

sections.heading: 7. Hipcamp: private land with rig limits
body: Hipcamp books stays on farms, stations, vineyards and bushland on private land. The app is free and rated 4.8 from 22,592 Australian ratings, and you pay per booking. A March 2026 update renamed its RV filter to rig type and made listings clearer on whether a site is 2WD accessible, 4WD recommended or 4WD required.
It is built around bookable stays, so it is not the app for finding dump points, rest areas or free camps between them.

sections.heading: Also worth knowing
body: G'day Parks books its own network of holiday parks, more than 350 by its listing, and its G'day Rewards membership costs A$50 for two years with 10% off bookings, up to A$50 each. Caravan Helper costs A$4.99 and lists dump points from the National Public Toilet Map and travellers, with payment and key requirements.

For weights, loadmate checks a rig against its rated limits but has only a handful of ratings so far, and ExplorOz Traveller suits off-road vans on remote tracks, at A$59.99, plus an in-app upgrade for full-detail topo maps without signal (from A$59.99 a year, or A$79.99 for a four-year edition).
tips: loadmate and ExplorOz for weights and tracks

sections.heading: Check your weights before the apps
body: No app knows what your van weighs once it is loaded. The NSW Government's towing page says the loaded trailer must not exceed the lowest of the towbar and coupling rating, the vehicle's towing capacity, the trailer's own carrying capacity and the tyre ratings, and that about 5 to 10 per cent of the loaded trailer's mass should sit on the coupling. Brakes depend on the gross trailer mass: none are required up to 750 kg, and a trailer with a gross trailer mass over 2 tonnes needs brakes on all wheels and an automatic breakaway system.
Our guide to towing a caravan covers licences, the four load limits and towing speed limits in WA and NSW.
tips: About 5 to 10 per cent on the coupling

sections.heading: How we compared them
body: Each app's price, in-app purchases, rating and version were checked on the Australian App Store on 20 October 2026, and features and offline behaviour on each developer's own pages. We looked at what a caravan or motorhome needs: whether a site suits the rig, where to empty and refill, and what still works out of signal. Where a developer does not document a feature, we have said so rather than guessed.

AussieCamps is our own app, and its camping data is sold through the Pass. No other developer paid to be in this comparison. If a price or feature has changed since then, let us know on the support page.

faq: What is the best app for caravanning in Australia?

It depends on the question you need answered. CAMPS Australia Wide filters sites by set-up, including big rigs, AussieCamps uses official data for dump points, water and rest areas on iPhone, and WikiCamps has more than a million traveller reviews by its own count. Many caravanners pair one of these with a navigation app.
Is there an app that shows big rig friendly campsites?

CAMPS Australia Wide lets you filter by camping set-up, including big rig, and shows big rig access on its dump points. WikiCamps lists site features for vehicle access, recorded by its users. Hipcamp has a rig type filter for its private-land stays. Check the site details before you commit to a narrow track.
What is an RV Friendly town?

A town in the CMCA's RV Friendly program, which offers short-term, low-cost overnight parking of 24 or 48 hours for self-contained recreational vehicles, plus drinking water and a free dump point. CMCA publishes a map of them.
Do caravan apps work without phone signal?

Partly. CAMPS, WikiCamps, CamperMate and CMCA Traveller let you download maps or site data before you go, and AussieCamps keeps place details on the phone. Live maps, routing and weather still need signal in most apps.

best-apps-working-holiday-australia.title: Best Apps for Working Holiday Makers in Australia 2026: 13 Picks
best-apps-working-holiday-australia.description: The apps a 417 or 462 visa holder actually uses in 2026: myVEVO, the ATO app, Record My Hours, SEEK, The 88th Day, AussieCamps and more, with the rules behind them.
best-apps-working-holiday-australia.imageAlt: Rows of banana plants with bagged bunches on a plantation near Cardwell, Queensland
best-apps-working-holiday-australia.intro: A working holiday in Australia runs on a handful of apps: one to prove your work rights, one for tax, one to find work that counts towards another visa, one to log your hours, and a few for getting between jobs. Several of the most useful are free government apps. AussieCamps is our own app, which is why it comes first, and each entry says when another app would serve you better. Every app was checked on the Australian App Store on 20 October 2026, and the rules come from Home Affairs, the ATO and the Fair Work Ombudsman.

sections.heading: Quick comparison
body: The apps fall into four jobs: staying legal, getting paid correctly, finding work and getting around. You will want at least one from each.

sections.heading: 1. AussieCamps: where to stay between jobs
body: Regional work means long drives between towns where accommodation is thin. AussieCamps puts bookable hotels, motels, backpacker hostels, holiday parks and tours from BookEasy in one iPhone app, free to browse and book, so you can find a bed near the next farm without paying for the app first.

If you are travelling in a car or van, the AussieCamps Pass adds 1,838 campgrounds, 5,552 rest areas, 3,004 drinking water points and 1,186 toilets from state park agencies, road authorities and public facility datasets, and trips with the distance and drive time between stops. Place details are stored on the phone and stay readable out of signal; the map, directions and weather need a connection. The Pass is a weekly subscription or a one-off lifetime purchase, with in-app purchases listed at A$2.99 to A$9.99.
The app runs only on iPhone, and it carries no traveller reviews. If you only ever stay in hostels in cities, Hostelworld covers more of them, with reviews from other backpackers.
tips: Hostels and holiday parks free to browse and book
Campgrounds and rest areas need the Pass

sections.heading: 2. myVEVO: check your work rights
body: myVEVO is the free Home Affairs app for checking your visa's work rights, conditions and expiry date. It lets you email your visa details straight to an employer, and Home Affairs says employers can check your work rights through VEVO with your permission. It is rated 4.8 from 4,420 Australian ratings.

Home Affairs says working holiday makers can usually work for the same employer for 6 months only, counted from your first day and including part-time, casual and voluntary work. You can work for the same employer for more than 6 months without asking permission if you work in different locations, none of them for more than 6 months, or in plant and animal cultivation, or in critical sectors including tourism and hospitality, agriculture and aged care, anywhere in Australia, among other exceptions. It is free on iPhone and Android, and the same check is on the VEVO website.
tips: Email your visa details to an employer

sections.heading: 3. The ATO app and myGov: tax and super
body: You apply for a tax file number online with the ATO once you are in Australia on a visa that lets you work. Give your employer the number: without it, the ATO tax table says they must withhold 45%. The ATO app then shows your tax and super, but to see your own records it needs a myGov account linked to the ATO and an Australian mobile number, so set those up in your first week. The myGov app handles sign-in and government mail.

Working holiday makers are taxed at 15% on income up to A$45,000 in 2025-26 and 2026-27. Only an employer registered with the ATO as an employer of working holiday makers can withhold at that rate; an unregistered employer must withhold 30%, and any extra is refunded when you lodge your return. When you leave, you can claim your super as a Departing Australia Superannuation Payment, with the taxable part taxed at 65% if it includes super paid while you held a 417 or 462 visa. Both apps are free; their ratings are low, 2.7 for the ATO app and 2.3 for myGov.
tips: Apply for a TFN once in Australia
15% up to A$45,000 with a registered employer

sections.heading: 4. Record My Hours: proof of what you worked
body: The Fair Work Ombudsman's free Record My Hours app records your shifts, automatically by location or entered by hand, and stores photos of your payslips. If your pay looks wrong, that record is what you take to the employer or to Fair Work. It is on iPhone and Android, and rated 2.4 from 88 Australian ratings.

Visa holders have the same workplace rights as every other employee. On farms covered by the Horticulture Award, pieceworkers must be paid at least the minimum hourly rate for the hours they work each day, a guarantee that has applied since April 2022. The app records hours; it does not work out your award pay.
tips: Free, from the Fair Work Ombudsman

sections.heading: 5. SEEK: the most-rated job board app
body: SEEK has more Australian ratings than any other dedicated job app here, 422,409 averaging 4.7, and covers hospitality, farm, retail and trade work in every state. It is free on iPhone and Android.
It is not built for working holiday makers, so listings do not say whether a job counts as specified work for another visa. Check the industry and postcode against Home Affairs before you accept.

sections.heading: 6. Indeed and Jora: more of the market
body: Indeed (4.7 from 51,502 ratings) and Jora (4.7 from 78,753) are free job search apps. Jora pulls roles from company sites, recruiters and other boards across Australia, New Zealand and Singapore, so one search covers many boards.
The same job can appear on several boards. Like SEEK, neither tells you whether a role counts towards a second or third visa.

sections.heading: 7. Workforce Australia: the government jobs board
body: The Australian Government's Workforce Australia jobs board includes harvest and farm work, and its free app searches by industry, location and the days you can work. It is rated 3.4 from 4,737 Australian ratings.
It is built mainly for Australian jobseekers, so some of its features may not apply to you, but its harvest listings are worth checking alongside the private boards.
tips: Free, from the Department of Employment

sections.heading: 8. The 88th Day: finding specified work
body: The 88th Day is built for working holiday makers chasing the regional work for a second or third visa. It has a database of farms and factories for finding specified work, mostly around Adelaide and South Australia, and a calculator for counting your days. It is rated 4.6 from 459 Australian ratings and free to download, with in-app purchases from A$6.99 to A$19.99 for nationwide, full or premium access.
An employer appearing in an app does not make the work eligible. Eligibility depends on the industry, the postcode and your visa, so check each job against the Home Affairs list.

sections.heading: 9. Hostelworld and CamperMate: getting around
body: Hostelworld is a hostel booking app rated 4.8 from 28,649 Australian ratings, with reviews from other guests. CamperMate is free with no in-app purchases and lists free camps, holiday parks, toilets and dump stations across Australia and New Zealand, with maps you can download before you lose signal.

Hostelworld is built around hostels, with some budget hotels and B&Bs. Many of CamperMate's listings and updates come from travellers, so check a free camp's rules on the sign or with the land manager.

sections.heading: 10. Gumtree: buying a car or van
body: Many working holiday makers buy a car or van second-hand, and Gumtree, rated 4.7 from more than 1 million Australian ratings, is where many of them are listed, along with rooms and casual jobs.
Inspect the vehicle in person and check its registration and history before you pay.

sections.heading: The rules behind the apps
body: To get a second Working Holiday visa you need at least 3 months of specified work, a minimum of 88 calendar days, and for a third visa at least 6 months, a minimum of 179 calendar days. As a rule, the work must be done while you hold your previous visa: your first visa for a second, and your second visa, on or after 1 July 2019, for a third. Paid work must be paid under Australian law and awards (some volunteer disaster recovery work also counts), and the eligible industries and postcodes differ between the 417 and 462 visas. UK passport holders who apply on or after 1 July 2024 do not need specified work for a second or third 417 visa.

In September 2026 the government announced a plan to allocate second and third visas by ballot, with the regional work still required to enter. It was not in force and had no start date when we checked, so confirm the current rules with Home Affairs before planning around it.

body: Each app's price, in-app purchases and rating were checked on the Australian App Store on 20 October 2026. The rules come from the Department of Home Affairs, the Australian Taxation Office and the Fair Work Ombudsman, and the visa rules change often, so check them before you rely on them.
We built AussieCamps, and the Pass is how we charge for its camping data. No other app or developer in this list paid to be included.
tips: Check before you rely on them

faq: What apps do I need for a working holiday in Australia?

Start with the free government apps: myVEVO for your visa conditions, myGov and the ATO app for tax and super, and the Fair Work Ombudsman's Record My Hours for your shifts. Add a job app such as SEEK, Indeed or Jora, and an app for places to stay, such as AussieCamps or Hostelworld.
How do I prove my work rights to an employer?
Use myVEVO, the free Home Affairs app, to see your visa conditions and email them to the employer. Employers can also check your work rights through VEVO online with your permission.
How many days of farm work do I need for a second year visa?

At least 3 months of specified work, a minimum of 88 calendar days, in an eligible industry and postcode for your visa. A third visa needs 6 months, at least 179 calendar days. UK passport holders applying for a 417 on or after 1 July 2024 are exempt.
What tax do working holiday makers pay in Australia?

15% on income up to A$45,000 in 2025-26 and 2026-27, with higher rates above that. Your employer withholds at that rate only if registered with the ATO as an employer of working holiday makers, and must withhold 45% if you give no tax file number.

best-weather-apps-camping-australia.title: Best Weather Apps for Camping in Australia 2026: BOM and 6 Others Compared
best-weather-apps-camping-australia.description: BOM Weather, WillyWeather, Weatherzone, Windy, Elders and more compared for camping and road trips: warnings, radar, fire danger, tides and what works without signal.
best-weather-apps-camping-australia.imageAlt: Storm clouds and rain falling over Kata Tjuta at sunset in the Northern Territory
best-weather-apps-camping-australia.intro: On a camping trip the forecast decides more than the itinerary: whether to pitch on the beach, cross a causeway, light a fire or move on before a storm. Most of the apps here start from Bureau of Meteorology data, but they differ in warnings, radar, tides and what they keep when the signal drops. BOM Weather comes first here because it carries the Bureau's own warnings. We make AussieCamps, which shows forecasts for campsites but is not a weather app; it is covered after the weather apps. Every app was checked on the Australian App Store on 20 October 2026.

sections.heading: Quick comparison
body: Install BOM Weather whatever else you choose: it is free and carries the official warnings. Add a second app for the job it does better, such as tides, wind or lightning.

sections.heading: 1. BOM Weather: the official warnings, free
body: BOM Weather is the Bureau of Meteorology's own app, which it calls Australia's official weather app. It is free with no ads on iPhone and Android. It gives hourly forecasts for 72 hours and a 7-day forecast, a rain radar from 90 minutes in the past to 90 minutes ahead, and active warnings on the map.

For camping, three features matter most. Warning notifications cover up to 3 locations and include fire weather, flood, heatwave, severe thunderstorm, tropical cyclone and coastal hazards. The fire danger rating for the district is shown in the app. And an offline mode keeps recently viewed data, so check your next camp before you lose signal.
Lightning is not among the features the Bureau lists for the app, and WillyWeather goes further on tides and swell, which is where the next apps help.
tips: Fire danger rating in the app

sections.heading: 2. WillyWeather: tides, swell and wind for coastal camps
body: WillyWeather builds its 7-day forecasts on Bureau data and adds tide times for every Australian beach and many rivers, swell height and direction, wind and an hourly UV forecast. It shows Bureau warnings for your location and lists campgrounds among more than 30,000 locations. It is rated 4.7 from 366,237 Australian ratings, on iPhone and Android.
The free app shows ads. WillyWeather+ costs A$6 a month or A$48 a year and adds custom alerts, rain projections and offline forecasts, a paid feature that helps when you camp out of signal.

sections.heading: 3. Weatherzone: lightning and the long view
body: Weatherzone's free app has radar with a lightning layer, a 10-day forecast, 28-day temperature and rainfall outlooks, marine conditions and widgets, and it lists official severe weather alerts. It has the most Australian ratings of the apps here, 598,996 averaging 4.6.

Pro costs A$5.99 a month and adds rain, storm and lightning alerts and individual lightning strikes; removing ads costs A$5.99 a year. Its forecasts are increasingly Weatherzone's own rather than the Bureau's, according to the data sources page of Elders Weather, which uses Weatherzone content, while radar and warnings still come from the Bureau.

sections.heading: 4. Windy.com: wind and storms in detail
body: Windy shows more than 50 map layers from global and regional models, including ECMWF, GFS, ICON and the Australian ACCESS-C, with a lightning tracker and alerts when strikes come close. It is rated 4.8 from 22,509 Australian ratings. Premium in-app purchases are listed from A$4.99 and add a 15-day outlook and more frequent updates.

It is the app for wind: gusts on an exposed headland, a rooftop tent or an awning. Its forecasts come from its own mix of models rather than from the Bureau, so use it alongside BOM Weather for official warnings rather than instead of it.

sections.heading: 5. Elders Weather: built for the bush
body: Elders Weather comes from the rural services company Elders and uses Bureau data and Weatherzone content, and its detail shows it: a 7-day forecast with frost risk and 9am and 3pm winds, a 48-hour forecast, radar, warnings and long-range rain maps. Silver membership, A$2.99 a year, adds 28-day and 12-month rainfall outlooks and lightning on the national radar. It is rated 4.5 from 67,905 Australian ratings.
It suits inland and rural trips, where frost and rain on dirt roads matter more than tides.

sections.heading: 6. AUS Rain Radar (Old BoM Radar): just the radar
body: AUS Rain Radar is an independent app, not from the Bureau, that shows local and national rain radar in the style of the old BoM radar, with a 7-day forecast. Some of its data comes from the Bureau. It is free with ads, or A$4.99 once to remove them, and rated 4.6 from 70,290 Australian ratings.
Its listing does not mention warnings, so treat it as a quick radar check.

sections.heading: 7. Apple Weather: already on your iPhone
body: Apple Weather is built into every iPhone and rated 4.8 from 118,616 Australian ratings. It gives hourly and 10-day forecasts and a precipitation map without installing anything.
Apple Weather can show severe weather alerts, but Apple does not name its Australian source, so use BOM Weather for the Bureau's official warnings.

sections.heading: AussieCamps: the forecast for each campsite
body: AussieCamps is a camping app rather than a weather app, but weather is part of every place page: current conditions and a 7-day forecast from Apple Weather for each campground, rest area and park. Add campsites to a trip with arrival dates and it shows the forecast for each stop you will reach within the forecast range, so you can see which night of the week looks wet before you book.

Forecasts need a connection, while place details such as facilities and fees stay readable out of signal. It has no warnings, radar or fire danger ratings, so keep BOM Weather alongside it. It is free to download, with in-app purchases, and runs on iPhone only.

sections.heading: Warnings, fire danger and the apps that carry them
body: Weather apps tell you what the sky will do; emergency apps tell you what the fire and emergency services are doing about it. The Australian Warning System uses three levels across bushfire, flood, storm and extreme heat: Advice, Watch and Act, and Emergency Warning.

Fire danger ratings run from Moderate through High and Extreme to Catastrophic, with No rating on low-risk days. State and territory fire agencies set them, and those agencies are also responsible for a total fire ban, so check the agency for the state you are camping in, not only a weather app. Emergency+ is free, helps you call Triple Zero (000) and shows your location details to read to the call-taker.

faq: What is the best weather app for camping in Australia?

Start with BOM Weather: it is free, carries the Bureau of Meteorology's warnings with notifications, and shows the radar and the district fire danger rating. Add WillyWeather for tides and swell at coastal camps, or Weatherzone or Windy for lightning and wind.
Does the BOM Weather app work offline?
Partly. Its offline mode shows the data you viewed recently, so open the forecast for your next camp before you lose signal. New forecasts, radar and warnings need a connection.
Which weather app shows lightning in Australia?

Weatherzone's free radar has a lightning layer, and its Pro subscription adds individual strikes and lightning alerts. Windy has a lightning tracker with alerts when strikes come close, and Elders Weather's Silver membership adds lightning on the national radar.
Where do I check fire danger and total fire bans?

BOM Weather shows the fire danger rating for your district. State and territory fire agencies set those ratings and declare total fire bans, and state apps such as VicEmergency show total fire ban status.

A few apps cut each of them, and most are free. AussieCamps is our app and comes first, for the reasons in its section; every other entry says what it saves and what the catch is. sections.heading: 1. AussieCamps: cut what you pay for a bed
body: On a long trip, nights add up faster than anything else, and the cheapest bed is often a campground run by a park agency, or a rest area where the sign allows an overnight stop. AussieCamps lists 1,838 campgrounds from park agencies and 5,552 rest areas from road authorities, and you can filter places by cost, including free and donation sites. Place pages show the prices the source reports, such as a fee per night, per person or per vehicle, so you know what a site costs before you drive in.

It helps with the second bill too. A trip in AussieCamps shows the distance and drive time between stops, which is what a fuel budget is built on, and it marks 3,004 water filling points and 1,186 toilets, so you are not buying bottled water or paying for a powered site just to use the facilities.
AussieCamps is free to download, with in-app purchases, and runs only on iPhone. It has no fuel prices or traveller reviews; for those, use the apps below.
tips: Filter by cost, including free sites

sections.heading: 2. Petrol Spy: fuel prices across state lines
body: Fuel is the second big bill. Petrol Spy shows prices on a map for Queensland, South Australia, New South Wales, Western Australia, Tasmania and the Northern Territory, using official feeds such as FuelCheck and FuelWatch, with price-cycle graphs for the eight capitals and alerts for a good time to buy. It is free with ads, or A$2.89 a year without them, and rated 4.8 from 184,903 Australian ratings.
In Victoria its prices are submitted by users, so the state's own Servo Saver is the better source there. Our comparison of fuel price apps covers each state in detail.
tips: Most states in one free app

sections.heading: 3. State fuel price apps: the official numbers
body: Several states publish station prices themselves, free to use. FuelCheck covers New South Wales and the ACT, Servo Saver sits in the Service Victoria app, FuelWatch publishes Western Australia's prices for the next day from 2:30pm, and FuelCheck TAS and MyFuel NT cover Tasmania and the Territory.
Each covers one state, so on an interstate trip a national app such as Petrol Spy saves switching.

sections.heading: 4. My 7-Eleven: lock in a fuel price
body: The My 7-Eleven app's Fuel Price Lock finds the cheapest of up to five nearby 7-Eleven stores within 250 km and holds that price for 7 days, at any 7-Eleven selling that fuel. Under terms last updated in February 2024, the saving is capped at 25 cents a litre and covers up to 150 litres per fill, with one lock open at a time and up to two in 24 hours. The app is free and rated 4.8 from 269,554 Australian ratings.
It compares 7-Eleven's own stores only, not other brands, so check a fuel app before you lock in.

sections.heading: 5. Flybuys and Everyday Rewards: points on what you buy anyway
body: The two big supermarket loyalty programs are free to join and work through their apps. Flybuys, linked to Coles, shows personalised offers for bonus points and lets you choose a fuel offer: points or 4 cents off a litre at Coles Express and Reddy Express. Everyday Rewards, linked to Woolworths, gives points on every shop at Woolworths and partners, with offers you can boost.
Points build up slowly on a short trip, so treat them as a bonus rather than a reason to shop: scan the card at the checkout and take the fuel discount when you fill up anyway.
tips: Flybuys fuel offer: 4 cents a litre

sections.heading: 6. WiseList: compare the supermarkets
body: WiseList compares Coles, Woolworths and ALDI prices as you add items to a shopping list, alerts you when items on your watch list go on special, and flags rare specials. It is free with ads. WiseList+ costs A$7.99 a month or A$49.99 a year and adds splitting a list by store, barcode scan and compare, and sending a list to a Coles or Woolworths online cart. It is rated 4.4 from 1,805 Australian ratings.
On a road trip, the free list comparison is the part that saves money: one stock-up shop in a bigger town usually costs less than topping up at a roadhouse.
tips: Paid tier adds scan and compare

sections.heading: 7. Woolworths and Coles: the specials and the list
body: Both supermarket apps show the weekly catalogue specials and let you build a shopping list; the Woolworths list shows your total spend before you shop, and both find an item's aisle in your local store. They are free, rated 4.6 from 120,022 (Woolworths) and 4.7 from 61,703 (Coles) Australian ratings.
Each shows one chain only, so pair one with WiseList if you want to compare.

sections.heading: 8. ALDI Australia: the Special Buys
body: The ALDI Australia app shows its Special Buys, which change on Wednesdays and Saturdays, sends notifications when new ones arrive and finds your nearest store. Its listing describes browsing specials and a store finder rather than online shopping. It is free and rated 4.8 from 10,919 Australian ratings.
Special Buys are limited-stock items, so the alerts matter if you are after something specific, such as camping gear.

sections.heading: 9. Too Good To Go: cheap food that would be thrown out
body: Too Good To Go sells surprise bags of unsold food from cafes, bakeries, restaurants and grocers, from A$6.99 a bag, collected at a set time. It started in Melbourne and then Sydney. It is free, with no in-app purchases, and rated 4.9 from 58,393 Australian ratings.
The contents are a surprise and the pick-up windows are fixed, so it suits a few days in a city better than a day on the highway.

sections.heading: 10. EatClub: discounts on eating out
body: EatClub offers up to 50% off the bill at restaurants with spare tables, applied when you pay with its digital card, with no booking fees or vouchers. It covers venues in most mainland states and lists more than 10,000 restaurants across Australia, the UK and New Zealand. The app is free, with an optional subscription listed at A$11.90 a month, and rated 4.8 from 9,482 Australian ratings.
Deals depend on which venues have spare tables at the time, so the choice changes through the day.

sections.heading: 11. Wise: fewer fees on your money
body: For overseas visitors, bank fees on every card payment and cash withdrawal add up over a long trip. Wise holds money in 40 currencies at the mid-market exchange rate and gives you a debit card. On its Australian pricing page, the card costs A$10, paying in the account's currency is free, and the first A$400 of cash withdrawals each month is free, with 2.69% charged above that.
Fees and products depend on the country your account is opened in, so open it in your home country and check the fees there before you travel.

sections.heading: 12. Splitwise: share costs fairly
body: Travelling with friends, the money leaks out in small shared costs: fuel, groceries, camp fees. Splitwise records who paid what in any currency, works offline and settles up at the end. It is free, with Pro in-app purchases, and rated 4.4 from 3,710 Australian ratings.
It records what people owe; you settle up in cash or by bank transfer.

sections.heading: Also worth knowing
body: ShopBack and TopCashback pay cashback on online bookings such as hotels and flights, but the money arrives only after the retailer confirms the purchase and is paid to an Australian bank account or PayPal. Foody Bag sells surplus food bags at a third of their retail price, mainly in Perth.
Half Price, a popular grocery specials app, had not been updated since March 2025 when we checked, so we have left it out of the main list.

body: We started from the bills that make up most of a trip budget, then checked each app's price, in-app purchases, rating and terms on the Australian App Store and the developer's own pages on 20 October 2026. Savings depend on how you travel, so each entry gives the catch as well as the saving.

faq: What apps save money when travelling in Australia?

Start with the biggest bills. AussieCamps finds free and low-cost campgrounds and shows their reported fees, Petrol Spy and the state fuel apps find cheaper fuel, WiseList compares Coles, Woolworths and ALDI, and Too Good To Go and EatClub cut food costs in the cities.
How can I save on fuel on an Australian road trip?

Check a fuel price app before you fill up: Petrol Spy covers most states, and New South Wales, Victoria, Western Australia, Tasmania and the Northern Territory run their own official fuel price apps. My 7-Eleven can hold a 7-Eleven price for 7 days, and Flybuys offers 4 cents off a litre at Coles Express and Reddy Express.
Which app compares supermarket prices in Australia?
WiseList compares Coles, Woolworths and ALDI prices as you build a shopping list, free with ads. Its paid WiseList+ tier adds splitting a list by store and barcode scan and compare.
Is there an app for cheap food in Australian cities?
Too Good To Go sells surprise bags of unsold food from cafes and bakeries from A$6.99, and EatClub offers up to 50% off the bill at restaurants with spare tables.

Through the park agency for that state or territory, such as NSW National Parks, Parks Victoria or Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service. In Queensland, every camp in a national park, state forest or recreation area needs a permit booked before you arrive.

Where else can I find farm stays in Australia?
AussieCamps lists bookable farm and station stays from BookEasy, and Airbnb and Stayz list rural cabins and farm stays too. Hipcamp remains the app built specifically around private-land camping.

best-apps-lap-of-australia.intro: A lap of Australia is long enough that no single app covers it. You need somewhere to stop each night, a map that works where the signal ends, fuel prices, weather and a way to plan the whole route. We make AussieCamps, and it comes first because stops and the overall plan are the first jobs of a lap; the rest of the list covers the jobs it does not do. All the prices, ratings and features in this list come from checks made on 21 October 2026.

sections.heading: What a lap of Australia asks of your phone
body: Long stretches between towns change what an app needs to do. Tourism Australia says services on the Nullarbor are often 150 to 200 km apart and advises you to top up whenever you have the chance, so fuel and the next stop matter more than they do on a coastal trip.
A lap usually needs five jobs covered: a place directory, an offline map, a fuel app, a weather source and a planner. No app here does all five, so the list is built to be mixed.
tips: Gaps of 150 to 200 km on the Nullarbor

sections.heading: 1. AussieCamps: where to stop, and a plan for the whole lap
body: A lap is a string of nights, and AussieCamps is built around finding them. It lists 5,552 rest areas, 1,838 campgrounds and 745 national parks, plus 1,393 dump points, 3,004 drinking water points and 1,186 toilets, from state park agencies, road authorities and public facility datasets, and you can filter by water, toilets, showers, power, dogs, vehicle access and fees.

Its trips let you add stops with dates, and it gives you the driving distance and time for each leg and for the whole journey, arrival dates with forecasts, a checklist and a packing list, with sharing and Calendar sync. The guides include road trips such as the Nullarbor crossing, Perth to Broome, the Darwin, Kakadu and Litchfield loop and the East Coast from Sydney to Cairns. Place details stay on the phone and can be read with no signal, while live maps, directions and weather need a connection.
AussieCamps runs on iPhone only, has no traveller reviews, no fuel prices and no offline map, and it is new, so it has no Australian rating yet.

sections.heading: 2. WikiCamps Australia: the big community directory
body: WikiCamps lists more than 65,000 sites by its own count, with reviews and photos from travellers, and costs A$9.99 once per platform. Its Trip Planner shows travel time and distance between stops, with fuel cost estimates, and its Offline Mode lets you explore sites and plans without reception. It is rated 4.5 from 16,662 Australian ratings.
It shows ads, listings are written by users, and version 6 is a rebuild that is still bringing features back, so treat it as a second opinion on a site, not the final word.
tips: Reviews of free and low-cost camps

sections.heading: 3. CAMPS Australia Wide: checked sites and state offline maps
body: CAMPS lists more than 16,000 sites its team says it has checked in person, with filters for campervan, camper trailer and big rig, price and pets, and live fuel prices. You download maps one state at a time over Wi-Fi, so choose the states you will cross next instead of all of them at once. It is free to download and free for 7 days, then A$14.99 a year, and it is rated 4.4 from 3,478 Australian ratings.
It is a subscription with no free tier after the trial, and downloaded maps need updating by hand to stay current.

sections.heading: 4. ExplorOz Traveller and Hema: maps for the remote stretches
body: Where the phone signal ends, a downloaded topographic map is what keeps you on the road. ExplorOz Traveller costs A$59.99, is designed mainly for offline travel with downloaded maps, lists more than 100,000 places and features routes such as the Canning Stock Route and the Great Central Road. Its full offline EOTopo maps are in-app purchases, and it is rated 4.3 from 1,353 Australian ratings.

Hema 4WD Maps costs A$99.99 on the App Store, with state topographic maps sold separately, and its listing was last updated in September 2022, so check it is current before you buy. Both are for the desert, Kimberley and Cape York sections more than for the coast road.

sections.heading: 5. Petrol Spy: fuel prices across the states
body: Petrol Spy compares real-time prices in Queensland, South Australia, New South Wales, Western Australia, Tasmania and the Northern Territory, and shows user-submitted prices in Victoria. It is free with ads, Premium is A$2.89 a year or A$14.99 for life, and it is rated 4.8 from 185,044 Australian ratings.
Its last update was in July 2025. New South Wales FuelCheck and Western Australia FuelWatch are official alternatives, and CAMPS also shows live fuel prices.

sections.heading: 6. BOM Weather: warnings you can rely on
body: The Bureau of Meteorology's own app is free and ad-free, with hourly and 7-day forecasts, radar, rain notifications and warnings, and an offline mode. It is rated 4.6 from 472,905 Australian ratings. For a lap it is the app to check for cyclone, flood and fire information as you cross regions and seasons.

sections.heading: 7. Google Maps and Apple Maps: navigation, with limits
body: Both are free and already on your phone. Google Maps lets you download an area for offline driving, but offline maps expire, there is no traffic offline, and its help page says a route holds up to 9 stops, so a full lap needs splitting into several routes. Apple Maps allows up to 14 stops on a route.
tips: Split a lap into several routes

sections.heading: Planning notes from the official sources
body: The Top End dry season runs from May to October and the wet season from November to April, when access to some remote attractions can be closed by flooding, so check road conditions before exploring remote areas or national parks. Interstate biosecurity rules are set by each state and territory, and travellers face on-the-spot fines for taking prohibited items across borders, so check what you are carrying.

Park rules differ too: Queensland needs a camping permit for every camp in its parks, booked before you arrive, and Tasmania needs a parks pass to enter its national parks. If you hire a vehicle for the lap, Camplify lists motorhomes and campervans from their owners, free to download and rated 4.6 from 527 Australian ratings.
tips: Dry season May to October in the Top End

sections.heading: How we chose
body: We picked the apps a Big Lap traveller needs for each job, and checked their price, rating, version and features on the Australian App Store and the developers' own pages on 21 October 2026. We left out Roadtrippers, whose listing describes it as a road trip planner for the USA and Canada.
We make AussieCamps and put it first; no other developer here paid to be included. Spotted something that has changed since? Say so on the support page.

faq: What apps do I need for a lap of Australia?

Most travellers combine a camp and stop directory such as AussieCamps, WikiCamps or CAMPS, an offline map for remote stretches, a fuel app, BOM Weather for warnings and Google or Apple Maps for navigation.
Which app is best for finding free camps on a Big Lap?
WikiCamps has the largest community catalogue of free and low-cost camps for A$9.99 once per platform, and CAMPS lists sites its team has checked for A$14.99 a year after a 7-day trial.
Do I need offline maps for a lap of Australia?
Yes for the remote sections. Tourism Australia says Nullarbor services are often 150 to 200 km apart, so download maps in Google Maps, CAMPS or ExplorOz while you still have coverage.
Is there an app that plans the whole Big Lap?

No single app plans every part. AussieCamps builds a trip of ordered stops with driving distance and time for each leg and forecasts for your arrival dates, and Google Maps limits a route to 9 stops, so a full lap is split into several routes.

best-dump-point-toilet-apps-australia.description: The best apps for finding dump points and public toilets in Australia in 2026, from the National Public Toilet Map to camping apps, compared on price, data and fees.
best-dump-point-toilet-apps-australia.imageAlt: A toilet block beside the road at the Mullengudgery rest area in New South Wales
best-dump-point-toilet-apps-australia.intro: Finding a dump point or a clean toilet is a daily job on a caravan or campervan trip, and several of the best apps for it draw on the same official source: the National Public Toilet Map. They differ in what else they show, what they charge and whether they cover dump points at all. We make AussieCamps, which keeps every dump point from that map next to campgrounds and rest areas, and we say below what it leaves out. The figures here come from App Store and developer pages read on 21 October 2026.

sections.heading: What to look for in a dump point or toilet app
body: The National Public Toilet Map, run by the Australian Government, lists more than 23,000 public and private facilities. Its data includes whether a site has a dump point, whether there is wash-out water, whether a fee or a key is needed and the opening hours. Several apps below use that data, including Convenience, Caravan Helper and AussieCamps, so the useful differences are the filters, the extra places and what the app costs.

One caution from the map's own release notes: its newer flags, including wash-out water, start as false until they are updated. A site with no wash-out flag means unknown, not that there is no tap, so check the sign on site.
tips: Several apps share the Toilet Map data

The dump points, water and toilets come from the National Public Toilet Map, and the campgrounds and parks from state park agencies, so one search covers where to empty, fill and sleep.

Place details are stored on the phone, so they stay readable with no signal; live maps and directions need a connection.

sections.heading: 2. National Public Toilet Map: the official source
body: The official National Public Toilet Map app is free, rated 4.6 from 9,975 Australian ratings, and covers toilets with adult change, baby care, accessibility, opening hours, hoists, sharps disposal and showers. It is the broadest list of toilets in towns, shopping centres and parks.

Its store listing focuses on toilets and does not mention dump points, although the map's data includes a dump point flag and the trade site RV Daily reports a dump point filter in its apps. Urban toilets also outnumber the roadside ones you want on a long drive.
tips: Dump points are a filter to switch on

sections.heading: 3. Convenience: toilets with key and payment filters
body: Convenience is free to download and shows more than 23,000 facilities from the government data, with key and payment requirements, parking and accessibility, and routes through Apple Maps or Google Maps. Including caravan and RV dump points is a Convenience Plus feature, also sold as a separate A$2.99 purchase, and the app has other purchases from A$1.99. It is rated 4.3 from 78 Australian ratings.
Its store page does not say whether it works offline.

sections.heading: 4. Caravan Helper: dump points only
body: Caravan Helper costs A$4.99 with no in-app purchases and does one job: nearby dump points with distance and travel time in a list or on a map, plus payment and key requirements and parking. Its database combines the National Public Toilet Map's dump points with ones from the community, and each shows how long ago it was last verified. It is rated 4.5 from 310 Australian ratings.
It is paid up front, covers dump points only, and does not state its offline behaviour.

sections.heading: 5. WikiCamps Australia: dump points inside the big directory
body: WikiCamps lists more than 65,000 sites by its own count, including dump points and showers, with filters for water refill, dump points and more. It costs A$9.99 once per platform, and its Offline Mode lets you use sites and up to three planned trips without reception. It is rated 4.5 from 16,662 Australian ratings.
We could not find a published dump point count, listings are written by travellers, and version 6 is a rebuild, and some recent reviews mention filters that are missing, so check what you rely on.

sections.heading: 6. CAMPS Australia Wide: dump points with fee and big-rig symbols
body: CAMPS lists more than 1,000 public dump points, with addresses, GPS co-ordinates and symbols for cassettes, holding tanks, big rig accessibility and fee amount, according to its developer. It is free to download and free for 7 days, then A$14.99 a year, with premium offline maps that include site information. It is rated 4.4 from 3,478 Australian ratings.
Its developer site says 1,400 and its App Store text says 1,100, so we state only that it is over 1,000. It is a subscription with no free tier after the trial.

sections.heading: 7. CamperMate: free, with dump stations and toilets
body: CamperMate is free with no in-app purchases and lists dump stations, public toilets, Wi-Fi spots and supermarkets across Australia and New Zealand. Its listing says you can download maps and use it without an internet connection. It is rated 4.4 from 1,543 Australian ratings.
It shows ads, and we could not find a published dump point count.
tips: Ads; dump point count not found

sections.heading: Fees and rules at dump points
body: Fees vary and no single national price exists. Many council dump points are free, such as the six public ones listed by the West Coast Council in Tasmania, while a park-run one can charge, as the Shire of Toodyay in Western Australia says Toodyay Holiday Park does for a small fee. Check the hours, whether a key or code is needed and whether there is a fee before you arrive.

Councils also set the rules. Singleton Council in New South Wales expects caravanners to use designated dump points for toilet cassettes and prohibits flushing waste down wash basins or toilets in ablution blocks. Rules on grey water and toilet waste differ by state and land manager, so check with them, and see our dump point guide for how to empty correctly.
tips: Rules set by councils and land managers

sections.heading: How we compared them
body: We checked each app's price, in-app purchases, rating, version and features on the Australian App Store and developer sites on 21 October 2026, and the data fields on the National Public Toilet Map's own documentation. We left out apps that were stale or aimed at the United States.
We make AussieCamps, which is why it opens the list; none of the other apps paid to be here. If a price or a feature has changed, tell us on the support page.

faq: What is the best app for finding dump points in Australia?

For one dedicated app, Caravan Helper is a A$4.99 dump point finder with community checks. Camping apps such as AussieCamps, WikiCamps and CAMPS list dump points beside campgrounds, and the National Public Toilet Map is the free official source.
Is there a free app for public toilets in Australia?
Yes. The National Public Toilet Map app is free, is run with the Australian Government's data and covers more than 23,000 facilities, with accessibility detail, opening hours and sharps disposal.
Do dump points cost money in Australia?
It varies. Many council dump points are free, and some park-run ones charge a small fee. Check the fee and whether a key is needed in the app or on the council page before you arrive.
Do dump point apps work offline?

Some do. WikiCamps has an Offline Mode, CAMPS has downloadable offline maps, CamperMate lets you download maps, and AussieCamps keeps place details on the phone while its map and directions need signal. Convenience and Caravan Helper do not state their offline behaviour.

best-national-park-apps-australia.title: Best National Park Apps in Australia in 2026: 6 Compared
best-national-park-apps-australia.description: The best national park apps in Australia in 2026: official park apps, trail and camping apps compared on price, coverage and offline use, with entry fee and closure sources.
best-national-park-apps-australia.imageAlt: Tents at the Mt Clear campground below the ranges of Namadgi National Park in the Australian Capital Territory
best-national-park-apps-australia.intro: Australia has no national park pass and no single national park app. Each state and territory runs its own parks, fees and bookings, and only a few agencies publish an official app. The useful apps are a mix: official ones where they exist, and camping and trail apps that cover parks everywhere. AussieCamps is ours and comes first because it covers the national parks of every state in one place, and we say what it leaves out. Prices, ratings and features were verified on 21 October 2026.

sections.heading: What a national park app can and cannot do
body: Parks are run by the agencies of each state and territory, so the official source for fees, bookings and closures is always the agency. NSW urges visitors to check for closures before heading out as conditions can change quickly, Victoria points you to the VicEmergency website and app for warnings, and Queensland publishes park alerts on its parks website.
An app is a planning aid. It can show where the parks, campgrounds and tracks are and what is there, and some work without reception, but confirm closures and fees with the agency before you travel.

sections.heading: The apps at a glance
body: Combine a broad app for finding parks and campgrounds with the official app for the park you are visiting, where one exists.

You can save parks into lists and collections, add them to a trip with dates and see the driving time between stops, and open directions in Apple Maps or Google Maps. Place details are stored on the phone, so they stay readable with no signal; live maps, directions, forecasts and photos need a connection.

sections.heading: 2. NSW National Parks: the official app for NSW
body: The NSW National Parks app is free, comes from the state's parks service and covers more than 225 national parks, with maps, things to do, campgrounds, caravan sites and cabins and the facilities in each park. You can download a park at home and view its information and maps during your visit, even without reception. It is rated 4.6 from 2,746 Australian ratings and is also on Android.
It covers NSW only, and bookings need an internet connection. NSW charges vehicle entry at 45 of its parks and reserves, per vehicle, and walkers and cyclists enter free.
tips: Download a park before you go

sections.heading: 3. Uluru and Kakadu: the two Parks Australia apps
body: Parks Australia runs Uluru-Kata Tjuta and Kakadu, and each has its own free app with maps of walking tracks and facilities, visitor guides, tours and events, and information on opening hours, park passes and safety. You can save favourites and download the app's content before you visit to use it offline. Each has only a handful of Australian ratings so far.

The passes are separate and each is valid for its own park only: Uluru is A$38 for 3 days for adults (18 and over), and a Kakadu pass is valid for 7 days, with the adult (16 and over) price A$25 from 1 November to 14 May and A$40 from 15 May to 31 October, and Northern Territory residents free. All other national parks in the Northern Territory are managed by the Northern Territory Government.

sections.heading: 4. AllTrails: walking tracks inside the parks
body: AllTrails is a trail app with reviews, conditions and turn-by-turn navigation, and its store listing says it has more than 500,000 trails around the world. It is free, with AllTrails Plus listed from A$35.99 and Peak at A$79.99, and Plus adds map downloads for trails, parks and whole areas. It is rated 4.8 from 33,117 Australian ratings.
It is a community app, not an agency one, and its store text does not mention park closures or fees, so check those with the agency.

sections.heading: 5. CAMPS Australia Wide: park campgrounds with offline maps
body: CAMPS lists national park campgrounds along with state forest and nature reserve camping, and its team says it has checked its sites in person. It is free to download and free for 7 days, then A$14.99 a year, with offline maps for when there is no signal. It is rated 4.4 from 3,478 Australian ratings.
It is a subscription with no free tier after the trial, and it is a camping app, so it will not show a park's tracks.

sections.heading: 6. More to Explore: Victorian state forests
body: Victoria's More to Explore app is free and covers more than 600 attractions in the state's forests, with the open or closed status of tracks and sites, filters for toilets and for small caravan and camper trailer access, and up to 15,000 square kilometres of offline maps. It is rated 2.8 from 116 Australian ratings.
It covers state forests, not Parks Victoria's national parks, so use Parks Victoria's website for those.

sections.heading: What parks charge to enter
body: There is no national pass, and fees are set by each agency. In Western Australia a standard vehicle pays A$17, the entry fee covers one or more parks on the same day, and walkers and cyclists are exempt. Tasmania's Holiday Pass covers all national parks for up to two months at A$98.35 per vehicle, and Tasmania's fees are reviewed each year in line with CPI.
Fees and rules change, so check the agency for the park you plan to visit. Our camping fees guide has the state-by-state detail.

sections.heading: How we compared them
body: We checked each app's price, rating, version and features on the Australian App Store on 21 October 2026, and the fees and closure rules on the park agencies' own pages. We found official apps for New South Wales, Uluru, Kakadu and Victoria's state forests in the Australian App Store, and none for the national parks of the other states, which does not prove none exists.
AussieCamps is ours and it comes first for the reasons in its section; nobody paid for a place in this list. If you spot a price or feature that has changed, tell us on the support page.

faq: Is there an app for Australian national parks?

There is no single national park app. NSW has an official app covering more than 225 parks, Parks Australia has apps for Uluru and Kakadu, and AussieCamps, CAMPS and AllTrails cover parks across the country.
Is there a national park pass for all of Australia?
No. Each state and territory sets its own entry fees and passes, and Uluru-Kata Tjuta and Kakadu have their own Parks Australia passes, each valid only for that park.
Do national park apps work offline?

Some do. The NSW National Parks app lets you download a park before you go, the Uluru and Kakadu apps let you download their content, and CAMPS has offline maps. AussieCamps keeps place details on the phone while its map, weather and photos need signal.
How do I check if a national park is closed?

Check the park agency, such as NSW National Parks, the VicEmergency website and app for Victoria, or Queensland's park alerts page. Apps can show where a park is, but the agency is the source for closures.

Its App Store listing was last updated in September 2022, and Hema has retired its Explorer Cloud platform, so check which Hema app is current before you buy.

sections.heading: 3. Newtracs: assessed 4x4 tracks, free to start
body: Newtracs is free to download, with Premium at A$19.99 a month or A$129.99 a year, and lists more than 13,000 assessed 4x4 trails and more than 8,000 campsites, parks, towns and places that you can search offline, with offline vector maps and crowd-sourced track ratings. It also shows a daily feed of Victorian track closures, and topographic detail is a Premium feature. It is rated 4.7 from 8,237 Australian ratings and also runs on Android.
It focuses on 4WD tracks, not on a general camp directory.

sections.heading: 4. CAMPS Australia Wide: checked camps and state offline maps
body: CAMPS lists camps its team says it has checked in person, with notes such as 4WD-only access and dry-weather conditions, and mobile coverage detail on site pages. You download maps one state at a time over Wi-Fi, and if you have not downloaded a state, the app reverts to basic offline maps with limited zoom. The download is free and the first 7 days cost nothing, after which it is A$14.99 a year; the rating is 4.4 from 3,478 Australian ratings.
It is a camping app, not a track-navigation or topographic one.

sections.heading: 5. WikiCamps Australia: reviews of remote camps
body: WikiCamps costs A$9.99 once per platform and lists more than 65,000 sites by its own count, with reviews and photos from travellers. Its Offline Mode lets you explore sites and your trip plans without phone reception. It is rated 4.5 from 16,662 Australian ratings.
It shows ads and listings are written by travellers, and it is not a topographic map app.

sections.heading: 6. Google Maps, Apple Maps and Organic Maps: free offline baselines
body: Google Maps lets you download an area for offline driving, but offline maps expire, can auto-update and have no traffic offline. Apple Maps offers offline maps with turn-by-turn driving directions on iPhone. Organic Maps is a free, ad-free app built on OpenStreetMap that describes itself as fully offline, and is rated 4.7 from 568 Australian ratings.
ExplorOz, Hema and Newtracs are built around 4WD tracks, so on a desert track we would keep these free apps as a backup, not the main map.

sections.heading: When ExplorOz is still the better choice
body: If you need offline topographic maps with 4WD tracks, your own routing, and a library of places and routes written for remote travel, ExplorOz does that and the others here do parts of it. Its EOTopo map is built to show remote tracks that mainstream maps often miss, and its offline EOTopo maps are not metered.
The cost is higher, and its base app only carries the overview maps offline, so budget for the full offline maps before you leave signal.
tips: Routes and places for remote travel

sections.heading: How we compared them
body: We checked each app's price, in-app purchases, rating, version and features on the Australian App Store and the developers' own pages on 21 October 2026, judging them on what an ExplorOz user needs: offline maps, tracks and stops.

We make AussieCamps and list it first as the stop planner, not as a map; no other developer here paid to be included. If an app has changed its price or its maps, tell us on the support page and we will recheck.

faq: What is the best alternative to ExplorOz?

For offline topographic maps, Hema 4WD Maps and Newtracs are the closest, and CAMPS and WikiCamps add offline camp data. AussieCamps is not an offline map, but it keeps rest area, dump point and water details readable on the phone.
How much does ExplorOz cost?
ExplorOz Traveller costs A$59.99. Full offline EOTopo maps are in-app purchases: Pro Access at A$99.99 a year, EOTopo Annual Access at A$59.99 a year, or a 4-year edition at A$79.99 once.
Is there a free alternative to ExplorOz?

Newtracs is free to download with a paid Premium tier and shows track difficulty ratings. Google Maps, Apple Maps and Organic Maps are free with offline areas, and are best kept as a backup in remote country.
Which apps work without phone signal in the outback?
ExplorOz, Hema 4WD Maps, Newtracs, CAMPS and WikiCamps all have offline modes or downloadable maps. AussieCamps keeps place details on the phone, but its map, directions and weather need signal.

wet-season-camping-top-end-northern-wa.title: Wet Season Camping: Top End and Northern WA 2026-27
wet-season-camping-top-end-northern-wa.description: What closes and what stays open when camping in the Top End and northern Western Australia from November to April: roads, Kakadu, Litchfield, the Gibb River Road, cyclones, crocodiles and stingers.
wet-season-camping-top-end-northern-wa.imageAlt: Green Nadab floodplain seen from the rock outcrops at Ubirr in Kakadu National Park, Northern Territory
wet-season-camping-top-end-northern-wa.intro: The Top End and the Kimberley do not shut for the wet season, but parts of them do, and the list changes from week to week. This guide sets out what the official agencies say about roads, parks, cyclones and wildlife between November and April, and where to check each day. We read every source on 21 October 2026, and where an agency publishes no fixed date we say so instead of guessing one.

sections.heading: When the wet season starts, and what the build-up is
body: Tourism NT says the Top End wet season, or tropical summer, stretches from November to April, and its green season guide puts the build-up from October to December. The Bureau of Meteorology says the northern wet season runs from about October to April in the far north of the Northern Territory, and that the monsoon normally arrives around Darwin in late December. It describes the build-up as the stretch before that onset, which is mostly inactive weather.

The official tropical cyclone season for the Australian region runs from 1 November to 30 April. Tourism NT gives typical wet-season conditions as 25°C to 33°C with humidity that can pass 80%, and says Darwin averages 429 mm of rain in January. In the Kimberley, the Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA) says the wet runs from November to April and the rain is “usually confined to short downpours in the late afternoon or evening” but very heavy.
Agencies draw the lines a little differently, so plan around ranges. Kakadu's Parks Australia calls the monsoon season Kudjewk and gives it as December to March.
tips: Build-up from October, monsoon from about late December
Rain is heavy but often falls in the afternoon

Months
